subtopic: REPEAL OF CHAPTER 36 OF THE STATUTES OF
speechtext:
This is a
very short bill. It asks for the repeal of the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act, which was passed in 1933, was of a temporary nature, and was never completed. Rules were to have been passed by order in council, but this was not done; no machinery is provided for the operation of the act. It has lent itself to a lot of fraud. A petition is made against a company; the company files a petition to fall under the act, and immediately proceedings in bankruptcy are stopped. No liquidator is appointed, no trustee, no inspector. No examination of the books is made; officers of the company cannot be examined under oath, and nobody knows what is what about the company. Public bodies such as the Montreal board of trade have passed resolutions asking for the repeal of this act, and there is a great deal of protest against it. It will be my intention to ask that the bill be referred to the committee on banking and commerce in order that men from Montreal and other cities may be called who want to come and speak in favour of the repeal of the act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO OPERATION OF CIVIL SERVICE ACT
APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO OPERATION OF CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
That a select special committee of the house be appointed to inquire into the operation of the Civil Service Act, and all matters pertaining thereto, with power to call for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath, and to report from time to time;
And that standing order 65 be suspended in relation thereto, and that the select special committee shall consist of twenty-five members and the following be appointed members of the said committee;
Messrs. Beaubien, Betts, Boulanger, Brooks, Clark (York-Sunbury), Cleaver, Deaehman, Donnelly, Elliott (Kindersley), Fournier (Hull), Glen, Golding, Green, Jean, Lacroix (Quebec-Montmoreney), Lawson, Maclnnis, MacNeil, McNiven (Regina City), Mulock, O'Neill, Poole, Pouliot, Stewart, Tomlinson.
He said: Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that at the first session of the present parliament I indicated that the government had the intention of appointing a special select committee to take into consideration the operation of the Civil Service Act. Owing to -the many committees appointed at the first session and the number of matters that came before the house for consideration by a new administration and a new parliament, it was not thought advisable or possible to appoint a committee at that session. Last session, as hon. members will recall, owing ,to the coronation and the imperial conference there was a desire to expedite the business of the house, and it was thought advisable not to appoint a committee at that time. The government is therefore .taking an early opportunity in this session of implementing the promise which was made, that a committee would be appointed in the course of the present parliament.
I believe it is a fact that there have been similar reviews of the operation of the Civil Service Act during most of the parliaments of recent years. One reason for periodic reviews is that the needs and conditions of the public service are continually changing; also, the personnel of the house is continually changing. It is important the service should conform to changing needs. It is moreover an advantage to new members as well as old members to have this opportunity of fully appreciating many of the questions which arise in the conduct of the public service, both from the point of view of the civil servants themselves and from the point of view of those who have to do with their appointment. It is in the public interest also that there should be periodical inquiries into such matters as the efficiency of the public administration, as well as the cost of that administration.
The fact that the government is proposing the appointment of this committee at this time does not mean that the government does not hold strong convictions with respect to the public service and the principles which should govern its status and conduct. It does mean, however, that the government believes it will be helpful alike to the government itself and to the service to have the various duties and obligations of the service carefully reviewed by hon. members of this house, so that their experience may be brought to bear upon the act as it now is, with a view to such revisions or modifications as may seem most advisable. I might add the appointment of this committee should expedite the sessional program through the opportunity it will afford of consideration by the committee of proposals with respect to the civil service already before the house, or ready to be brought up by reference to committee.
I might say that the government intends to recommend the appointment of another committee to deal with the Civil Service Superannuation Act. The superannuation act is more concerned with questions which are immediately financial and which are in part technical. It has therefore been thought advisable to have that act dealt with by a smaller committee. It will be general questions and proposals with respect to the public service that will come up for consideration by the committee now proposed.
As to the personnel of the committee, hon. members will realize that the names as set forth are in alphabetical order. There is no significance as to which name comes first or which comes last. The committee will manage its own affairs, in the selection of a chairman as in other matters, but I would say at once that an effort has been made, through the cooperation of the whips, to have the committee as representative as possible not only of the different parties in the house but of considerations of which a committee of the kind would wish to take account. I need not mention what they are. Inevitably there may be a feeling that some persons ought to be on the committee who are not. All have not been accommodated to the extent that the government would wish to accommodate them. However, this committee will be no different from others in the matter of permitting of changes in personnel in the course of its proceedings if that be thought advisable. I just wished at present to inform hon. members that the names here set forth are those that have been given to the government after consultations between the whips of the different parties. I do not think there is anything further I need say at this stage.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO OPERATION OF CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure every member of this chamber, as well as the country generally, will be pleased with the next to the last observation made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), that from the setting up of this committee there was nothing to be taken that might imply that the government had any doubt as to the necessity of maintaining the merit system and a civil service commission in this dominion at this time. There is no doubt that there has been much discussion, sometimes public and sometimes not, with respect to the civil service commission and its operations; and it is highly desirable, I personally believe, that at least once in the life of every parliament there should be a review of the operations of the act.
The Prime Minister referred to the fact that the proposed committee was not to deal with the financial side of the matter. I observe that that is so, and the only question I had in mind was whether or not under the terms of the reference, namely "to inquire into the operation of the Civil Service Act," the committee would be competent to inquire into whether or not the departments were under- or over-staffed, or whether public moneys were overexpended in any particular place. As it reads now I doubt whether it would be broad enough for that purpose. The "operation of the act" merely means its administration, how it operates in practice, not the sufficiency or insufficiency of the numbers of employees engaged in the public service. That is a matter which is not settled by the act itself but is determined by the ministers, by what they conceive to be the necessities of the public service and by the appropriation that is made by parliament to defray the cost of such public service. It would therefore seem to me, if it is thought desirable by the government so to do, that the terms of the reference should be modified or expanded; for I submit the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) would say that to inquire into the operation of the Civil Service Act, when the civil service commission itself has nothing to do with the determining of the numbers of people who are to be employed, would be hardly adequate to meet the situation as a whole. I merely mention this because I thought possibly the government was of the opinion that it was not desirable for this committee to consider such questions as the adequacy or inadequacy of the numbers employed in the departments; that that was a matter which more largely concerned perhaps some other branch of the

public service and which was to be considered from some other angle.
I can only say it is highly desirable that every section of the country and every party in the house should be represented, as it is here, on the committee, and that an endeavour should be made so far as it may be possible to conduct the inquiry into the operations of the act with only one object in mind, namely, the public good and the extent to which, either by amendment or by new legislation, we may be able to improve the efficiency of the civil service. I thought, and I still think, that the language is not broad enough to go beyond the question of mere administration, and that possibly the Prime Minister and his government were of the opinion that it would be desirable to deal with that from another angle altogether, having regard to the report on professional employees made some years ago, and other matters of the kind that should be dealt with in another way, even as superannuation, which is largely a financial matter, should be considered from another angle than that of the operation of the act itself.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say to my right hon. friend that there was no intention on the part of the government in any way to restrict the scope of the committee's activities in this matter. As a matter of fact, in speaking I think I made direct reference to the cost of services, which of course would include the numbers employed, and the amounts paid to -them. If during the course of its inquiry the committee should feel that there is undue restriction in its scope, it would have power to ask the house to enlarge its authority. I assure the house at once that that concession would be made.
The intention is to -have the scope of the committee's inquiry made as broad as possible, and not to limit it in any particular. The purpose of having the Superannuation Act made the subject of a separate committee was simply to ensure that one particular phase of civil service interest would receive a more detailed and careful examination by a committee appointed with reference thereto than would be possible under the general inquiry.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: Mr. Neill moves, seconded by Mr. Donnelly, that the petition presented yesterday and laid on the table of the house be read. Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

Motion agreed to.
(The Clerk Assistant read the petition as follows):
To the honourable the House of Commons in parliament assembled:
The petition of the undersigned residents of the province of British Columbia, humbly showeth:
That since time immemorial large runs of sockeye salmon have passed the southwest coast of Vancouver island thence passing into American waters in Puget sound and then back to Canadian waters to spawn in the Fraser river.
That for many years we have maintained in the neighbourhood of Sooke on the southwest coast of Vancouver island four or five fish traps and the Americans maintained in their waters in Puget sound several hundreds, with result that our percentage of the joint catch of that run would run about thirty per cent while theirs would be seventy per cent.
That, three years ago the Americans took out all their traps in Puget sound numbering 219 while we retained ours, with the result that our proportion of the joint catch jumped from thirty per cent to fifty per cent and even eighty per cent.
That, the fact that we have not taken out our traps has been used and will be used as a very strong argument by the American trap owners for permission to re-introduce traps on the American side.
That, it is very much to our interests that the American traps should not be re-introduced.
That, there is no truth in the allegation that traps are the only means by which salmon can be taken in our waters in that neighbourhood, as it has been demonstrated that it can be fished by seines, gillnets, and trollers, to which the Americans would have no objection as they use the same gear themselves.
That, the above refers to the sockeye run of salmon but traps are as undesirable as regards the spring and cohoe runs. These fish are heavy in spawn making their way to their spawning ground, swimming in shoals, following the coast line, keeping in shallow water and close in shore so that they fall an easy prey to the traps and comparatively few get by.
That, traps are the most destructive form of fishing known, as they are open day and night and catch every species of fish, large or small, that comes along whether they happen to be out of season or not. Nothing escapes them or gets through.
That, the abolition of traps would lead to the revival of fishing and employment of many local fishermen as was formerly the case, but who, finding their livelihood gone, have had to find other work, often on relief.
That, it would encourage the tourist fishermen who spend their money freely provided that they get good fishing and who to-day are too often disappointed at the present poorness of the fishing in those waters. It would make a great difference to the tourist traffic in the vicinity of Victoria.
That, the abolition of the traps would protect the run of fish, would increase employment instead of, as is the case, exploiting one of British Columbia's greatest assets for the sole benefit of a few.
That, the Associated Boards of Trade of Vancouver island at their annual meeting in June last passed a resolution asking for the abolition of fish traps.
Wherefore, your petitioners humbly pray that your honourable house may be pleased to order that no more fish traps licences shall be granted in British Columbia.
And, as in duty bound, your petitioners will ever pray.
(Signed by Geo. Harris and 9,594 others.) SUPPLY

Mr. Speaker, before Your Honour leaves the chair, and as the estimates of the Department of National Defence may be introduced, I desire to direct the attention of the government to certain considerations which arise in respect of any discussion of these estimates at this time.
There is grave concern throughout Canada as to the developing international trends, and the possible implications arising therefrom and which attend upon Canada's position in the League of Nations and the British commonwealth. For this reason, without any desire to add to the difficulties of the situation and with every desire to cooperate in the promotion of peaceful external relations for Canada, it is urged that the government should provide an opportunity for the discussion of the general policy proposed with relation to the defence of Canada.
Preparations for defence are necessarily the outcome of foreign policy. It is therefore desirable that the government should give whatever assurance may be possible, indicating that existing commitments and plans do not contemplate participation in external war. It is hoped that the minister will make a statement, before proceeding to the principal items of his estimates, as to the relationship of the defence program to needs which are solely Canadian. speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
There are five branches of the Department of Mines and Resources and it might be of value to the committee if I took a moment or two to deal with the particular functions performed by this branch. It will be noted there is an item covering the dominion observatory at Ottawa, as well as one covering the dominion astrophysical observatory at Victoria, British Columbia. These observatories have to do with astronomy and the exchange of information with other countries in respect of that science.
There is also the dominion water and power bureau, which has the administration of the Dominion Water Power Act and the Irrigation Act. About ten years ago there was a body set up known as the Lake of the Woods control board, which is included in this branch. Then there is the engineering and construction service which has to do mainly with the work carried on in the national parks of Canada, which are under the administration of this department. It has to do with the building of roads, the preparing of plans for buildings in the parks, and other work of this kind required in the Indian Affairs branch and in one or two other branches of the department. The work of the international boundary commission is under the direction of this branch.

The next item covers the hydrographic and map service. Prior to the formation of the Department of Mines and Resources and the Department of Transport, this branch was a part of the old department of marine. The hydrographic service covers the work carried out in the coastal waters of Canada to determine depths of water, proper charting and proper mapping according to information discovered by day to day testing and exploration. Also included in this service are legal surveys and map service. Provision is made for the printing of the publication of the Canadian Institute of Surveying. A small amount is provided for the payment of fees to examiners of dominion land surveyors. Briefly, this covers the general work of this branch of the department. The first item called. No. 149, has to do with what might be termed the head office expense of the administration of the branch.

The minister has explained the extent to which the various survey operations of the government have been drawn together; he has referred to the geodetic service, the international boundary work, the legal surveys and map service, and the hydrographic service. But there is still another branch of the department which has to do with geological and topographical surveys. Would the minister explain to what extent there is liaison between these branches and what arrangements have been made for the utilization of these surveys for military purposes? Is there a committee at work to draw' together all the surveying work of the department?

The geological service stands more or less by itself. For instance, there is no intimate relationship between that service and the hydrographic service. Geological surveys consist mainly of the examination of rock formations in order to determine the likelihood of minerals being found. That work is under the mines and geology branch in the department, but legal and hydrographic surveys and the preparation of plans for the building of Indian schools or houses for Indian agents and everything of that kind come under the supervision of this particular branch.

The minister has stated that of necessity the geological survey must be separate from the survey services for other purposes. Surely the geological information could be published on, say, a topographical map and thus avoid a duplication of services.
This branch has to do with the printing of maps prepared by the mines and geology branch, and also compiles various maps from existing base maps. Of course, we endeavour to avoid entirely

Supply-Mines and Resources
anything in the nature of duplication in the branch. Considerable progress has been made in the reorganization of this work but I do not say for one moment that this reorganization is completed. To get a large department like this functioning efficiently is not a matter of a week or a month or even a year. It is a case of steadily consolidating the work and weeding out any possibility of duplication. We are aiming to reach the greatest degree of perfection and economy that it is possible to reach. I do not know that there is anything further I can add in that regard.

Is the coordinating
committee still in operation? It was set up for the purpose of seeing that there should be no overlapping.

There is an interdepartmental committee that has to do with aerial survey's, for instance. Several departments, including ours, are represented on that committee. It aims to prevent duplication between departments.

Apparently this is the branch of the department having to do with road construction. Will the minister give us a statement as to the progress that has been made with the trans-Canada highway so that we may have some idea when the different gaps will be finished and what gaps there are at the present time?

The only- part of the
trans-Canada highway that this department has anything to do with, in addition to that section in the National parks, is the section being built in British Columbia to which reference was made a year ago, the section between Golden and Revelstoke. The other part of the trans-Canada highway, of course, has no relation whatever to this department. Perhaps the Department of Transport or the Department of Labour could give information in that regard, but so far as this particular section is concerned, between the points I have mentioned, the distance to be completed is about thirty-three and a half miles.
When will that be finished- this year?

It is very doubtful whether it will be completed this year; it will depend on the amount of money that may be voted for the work in the supplementary estimates- hon. members will recall that in the past the appropriations for this work have been voted in special supplementary estimates. I am informed that the construction remaining is very heavy and it is doubtful whether it will be completed this year. However, it certainly should be completed in the following year.
Can the minister give an estimate of what it will cost to complete that gap?
The amount estimated to complete the thirty-three and a half miles is $875,000.
Will this complete the trans-Canada highway from Vancouver to Fort William?

I think it will be possible to drive an automobile from Vancouver to Fort William over the trans-Canada highway when this section is completed. My recollection is that the section between Winnipeg and Fort William is passable. I believe you can get from Winnipeg to Calgary and from Revelstoke to Vancouver; I know that you can get from Golden to Calgary. It is a rather winding road in some places, but it is quite good.
Can the minister tell us how long the gap is in northern Ontario?

I cannot give that information. The question does not come within the purview of my department, and I have learned by experience to avoid very carefully any intrusion in respect of the affairs of other departments.
I hope it comes within the purview of some department.
I am quite certain the resources of this government are not so far exhausted that it cannot give my hon. friend the information, but I am sorry I cannot give it to him to-day.

Item agreed to.
Dominion observatory, Ottawa, $116,700.

On page 118 we find the details with reference to thirty-seven officials. What is being done by these thirty-seven officials in connection with the earthquake situation, of which a survey was promised last session? There was an earthquake in Hamilton the other day. Under this item I asked a similar question last year, and I think the minister might give us a short survey to indicate what is being done.

The observatory has apparatus for registering earth tremors. I believe they are so sensitive that they will detect tremors almost anywhere in the world, at any rate thousands of miles away. There have been a few earth tremors or slight earthquakes in eastern Canada in the past year, but I really do not know what the observatory can do about them. The officials can register
Supply-Mines and Resources

them, through the apparatus, and can give information as to their violence, but I am afraid that is about the limit of their power in the matter.

I notice in the estimates of this department that there are small items for temporary assistance. Can the minister tell us why there are items for temporary assistance in his estimates when I do not see any in any other part of the estimates?
It is for temporary employees in the observatory who have not been made permanent.

Will the minister be good enough to tell us exactly what the observatory does and has done? I have formed a definite opinion about it myself, but I should be glad to have the minister tell us what the observatory and its employees are doing.
The work of the observatory is wholly a contribution to science.

What is the contribution of this observatory?
Mr.CRERAR: I might read from a memorandum I have here. My right hon. friend smiles; well, I can smile back at him.
I would feel all the better for that.

So far as the practical work of the observatory is concerned, I do not profess to be a judge, but I quote from this memorandum:
From a practical point of view one of the most important lines of work of the observatory is the measurement of star-positions and the determination of time. The principal instrument used for this purpose is a telescope of moderate power mounted in the meridian, called a " meridian circle," with which observations are made on the stars every clear night. Other instruments are various clocks and chronographs. An electrical time service is supplied to the parliament buildings and generally to government offices at Ottawa, over 600 electrical dials, all controlled from the observatory, being installed for this purpose. There is also a radio time service for time-comparison with other American and European observatories.
It goes on to speak about the examination of the sun. I read only a short time ago some observations by a very noted astronomer in which he expounded the theory that sunspots and their duration had a definite effect on meteorological conditions, rainfalls, and so on. The observatory at Ottawa makes all these examinations, and exchanges the information with other observatories throughout the world, and thus a body of scientific information is gathered and analysed which leads to conclusions which in future will probably have a practical value, as they have had in the

past. The keeping of an accurate record of the time is also probably of some importance.
I confess that my right hon. friend has me backed up against the wall so far as a detailed knowledge of the work of this observatory is concerned. But the observatory has been in existence for a long time; it is making its contribution to science by the exchange of information it gathers with similar institutions elsewhere in the world, and on the whole, I think it is desirable that it should be continued.

What is
the number in the employment of that branch?
On the staff? There are thirty-seven in Ottawa.
Is any report published of their work, for the last hundred years or so?
An annual report is published, as well as, from time to time, bulletins dealing with special investigations they have made.
Has the report been laid on the table this year? I have not seen it.

I am informed that general survey of the work done is included in the annual report of the department. But there are other special reports which are available; they can be secured and laid on the table. If, for instance, we have violent earth tremors or matters of the kind, special bulletins may be published.

Like the minister I do not know a great deal abbut this work, but I have been wondering whether it should not be conducted in collaboration with one of our universities instead of being directly under government control. I know of observatories in other parts of the world which are part and parcel of the university. Is there any direct connection between the Ottawa and Victoria observatories and the universities in different parts of the country?

Most of the nations have services of this kind. Great Britain has; also, I am informed, Australia and other dominions. It is quite true that some universities also carry on observation work of this kind, but as a rule they are heavily endowed and so have the financial means to acquire all the equipment, some of it very expensive, that is necessary for their observations. But I doubt if there is any university in Canada that could carry on the work which is being done here and in the astrophysical observatory at Victoria, on their own resources, and I question

Supply-Mines and Resources
whether parliament would want to vote special sums to any university to do the work which is being carried on by the department.

I was not suggesting for one moment that we do away with the work which is now, being done by our observatories. But I was wondering, in view of what is happening in other countries where universities have their own laboratories for this class of work, whether we could not get better results for the amount of money we are spending if this work were coordinated with that of some of the large universities. I hardly expect the minister to be able to give an immediate answer to a question of this kind, but if there could be some coordination between our universities and the work done by our observatories we might get better results than we do by having the work isolated in the city of Ottawa.
I understand that none of the Canadian universities carry on work of this kind. McGill university, Montreal, however, carries on work relative to determination of time.
The university of Toronto, in a rather large way, with the Dunlop telescope.

Yes, but the universities are not equipped for it. For the moment they have not the trained staff which is necessary, and for that reason, at the present time at any rate, I do not regard the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North as really practicable.

I hope the time will never come when the cultural advancement of this country will depend entirely on the universities. From my point of view the government should lead in all these matters, and I cannot understand why we should not accept rightly expended moneys as the proper attitude of this country to its culture.

I notice that there are
twenty astronomers and one assistant. Are all these astronomers employed in Ottawa or are some of them sent to other parts of the dominion? It seems a pretty heavy staff to be working in and around Ottawa alone.

My hon. friend will notice that there is a reduction this year from the number employed a year ago. Occasionally some of these scientists leave Ottawa to make observations elsewhere, but the headquarters are here and the staff is attached to the observatory here.

These astronomers, I
assume, are well trained. With all due deference to the remarks that have been made, for the most part they are university or college trained men. Looking at the salaries attached to the various items, I should say that if these are well trained scientists they are getting exceptionally low salaries. It is almost a crime for a government to establish a precedent of this kind, in view of the training which apparently is required before a person can call himself an astronomer. Would it be possible to decrease the number of so-called astronomers and increase the calibre or the quality of those who are employed? Certainly the salary is not commensurate with the type of work which one assumes to be required of a person who can call himself an astronomer. I do not like to see a budget increase, but I certainly would suggest the possibility of doing something to make the remuneration of these officials more in keeping with the training they are supposed to have. By reference to other branches of the service it will be seen that they are getting no more pay than persons doing clerical work which does not call for exceptional qualifications. Would the minister give some intimation as to the necessary qualifications of an astronomer in the case of a vacancy? I should like to see some connection between the qualifications and the salary offered. If it is not sufficiently large something should be done to improve the remuneration of these particularly qualified men.

These positions come
under the civil service commission. The commission classifies them and in its wisdom fixes the salary range. If a position is to be filled the civil service commission sets the standard of examination to be passed before an appointment is made. Usually appointees are taken from students in universities who have specialized in mathematics; astronomy I believe is in large measure dependent on mathematical science.
As to the observation of the hon. member that the salaries paid are not in keeping with what scientists of this calibre should receive, I am not qualified to pass an opinion. It is greatly to the credit of scientists that the men who engage in the different branches of science are usually more interested in the work than in the remuneration. That of course is not an adequate reason for underpaying them, but I can only repeat that these positions are classified by the civil service commission and the remuneration fixed by their classification.

Lest there might be some impression that the men on the staff of this observatory are not quite up to the standard we should have, I may say that such is not the case. I am happy to say that I believe the standard of knowledge and ability of the men on this staff compares very favourably with that of any similar staff in the world.

I am inclined to agree with the minister in that respect, and I can also join in the applause of my friend to the left when he suggests that these men are doing a good piece of work and making a sacrifice in the positions they hold. It is a very similar attitude to that adopted towards the teaching profession, of which I happen to be a member. But I think that point of view is fast getting into disrepute, where people are working for the love of the work and not altogether for the remuneration involved. It is time we changed that attitude, and a good place to effect the change is in government service. It will be noticed that you have clerks in practically the same category as far as salary is concerned as an astronomer. Surely a person with the qualifications necessary for the work of an ordinary clerk should not receive almost the same salary as a highly trained specialist in the field of astronomy. There is not enough differentiation, not enough emphasis placed on the qualifications required.
I know the minister probably has very little to do with the remuneration for these various positions, but someone should do something about establishing a new scale of remuneration for government officials so that there will be a greater differentiation between highly trained experts and those who do not require the same degree of training and the same qualifications. I am hoping that in another year we may see an increase, not in the total but in the remuneration of those retained in the service. Such a scale of remuneration as now prevails does not give rise to continuity of service but rather to disruption of service. No trained scientist is going to stay with the government at that salary; he will look for a position elsewhere and take it at the earliest opportunity. The result will be constant change in the branch, which is not good for the service. More encouragement should be given to highly trained experts to take government positions and remain with them so that we may get the benefit of their training and experience. I am hoping that by another year we may see some improvement, particularly now that we have a committee appointed to inquire into the civil service. I am firmly convinced that the labourer is worthy of his hire, and I feel that not only 
these highly trained government servants but others as well are not receiving pay commensurate with the work we expect them to do. I am hoping that this government will take steps to see that there is some amendment in that respect, so that public servants who are required to do such important work will receive adequate remuneration and there will be some inducement for them to stay in the service.

Has the minister in his department officials who are drawing two or three or more salaries? I noticed, going through the public accounts, that there are officials who draw salaries from one department and perhaps in one, two, three or four other cases draw another salary for other matters.

If there are such I have not been able to find them. I do not think there are in effect. If such are found I can assure the hon. member they will not last very long. There are no such cases in this department.
The minister does know there are cases in other departments?
That is correct.
What are the educational requirements for this magnetic observer?
The qualifications? I have no more idea than my hon. friend has.
Do they have to have university education?

I am informed that the
magnetic observer does not require to have university standing. His business is to read the instruments and charge them with the rolls of paper on which the graphic record is made. I should think perhaps he would be a sort of general handy man in connection with the observatory work.

Does the work of this observatory require a staff on duty twenty-four hours a day? Is there any part of the day when there is not some of the staff engaged? Is everything suspended for part of the day?

They have regular hours, much in line with the hours established in the service, but some members of the staff are required to do their work at night. For instance, observations of the stars have to be carried on at night, and observations of the sun in the daytime.

There is no direct relationship. The meteorological service has agents in various parts of Canada to measure the velocity of wind, the rainfall, the temperature, and such meteorological phenomena as I have just mentioned, but that is rather apart from the kind of work that is done in the observatory.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister if he will do this: Will he just investigate that department? That is all. I do not want to say anything more; I just want to ask him if he will do that. This department cannot possibly function with the material it has to work with and be of any particular national use. You must have a telescope of power. We have not had a new telescope for I forget how long. We have a telescope which, if my memory serves me aright, is of very medium power, and in these days when large and powerful telescopes have taken the place of the instruments that formerly were in use it follows that the bulletins from a college such as Harvard or from the Victoria observatory, where we have a new telescope, or from the observatory at Mount Wilson, where they have a new telescope, so dwarf our telescope into insignificance, almost, as merely to mean-to make a comparison- that we are keeping up a carriage in the days of the automobile.
If the minister will just investigate that I will be content. I know what he will discover. It is perfectly useless to undertake to keep up an institution unless it is supplied with the necessary material to enable it to function usefully. I think the minister knows how true that is. One of the members was speaking about men working for salaries that are low. Men get into this position; they are in the civil service; it is a case of security. They know that at a given time they will get their superannuation, and if the country does no,t supply them with material with which to do 31952-44
the work of astronomers, they do the best they can for a little while and then sink into that quiet calm which you sometimes find so prevalent in the public service, the undisturbed calm of waiting for the day; not the final day-
The senate.

Very few of them see the senate, unless they are organizers of the Liberal party, and sometimes that involves a reduction in pay. At any rate, be that as it may, I want to point out to the minister that we should either maintain a service that is worth while or we should cease playing with it, making ourselves more or less ridiculous. Astronomy is one of the oldest of sciences. Astron-omera made tremendous contributions, not only to science but to practical things, arising out of the application of the principles which they have established by experiment and otherwise. It would take a long time indeed to tell about what the astronomer has contributed to the world, going back to days long before the clan Mackenzie were located in the highlands of Scotland. The result of what we are doing is purely negative. On the question of time they do make a contribution undoubtedly, but I am glad to see that the minister has lopped off four employees this year, because it is perfectly obvious that with the material at their hands we have entirely too great a staff. Either give them something to work with or do not keep them out there doing nothing, waiting for that day that comes to all.
I am not going to discuss the matter in detail, for reasons that are obvious, but I do ask the minister himself to investigate it. There is just as much need for putting in a charge here for temporary help as there is for putting a fifth wheel on a coach. You do not need any temporary help there. It is a convenience, a very great convenience too. I mean it is convenient to many people; almost as convenient, for instance, as that S3.000 for the assistant franchise officer, a post which was not filled for so long until after the last election.
The basis of all success in astronomical work is equipment. I do not care what genius you may have in the science of astronomy; unless you have the equipment you can do nothing. That is why the Dunlop telescope was of such very great value to the university of Toronto. That magnificent equipment now enables them to play a part in the scientific world; but did anyone ever point to any part we played in the scientific world with the equipment we have here? I believe they did detect a .tremor about the time of the Shaw report, but as far as any other tremors were concerned I understand there have been no evidences of them.

They have to do with the matter of looking after time; they have to do with the recording of earth tremors, and I understand that their seismographic instruments, if that is the correct term, are fairly modem and complete.

I do think that is making some contribution. However, I shall bear my right hon. friend's suggestion in mind, and do the best I can.

The minister has stated that the most important function of the observatory is the recording of time. I notice that last year there was one time observer who was paid $400, and that this year we have not any.
Yes, but he was only an observer.
He is not connected only with the determination of time. I understand that was a special amount given fol other observations. However, I must confess that I do feel like a fish out of water.
Some of them survive, you know.

I hope this one will, too. I feel that way when I am asked to discuss the scientific bases upon which time is determined, and all that sort of thing. It is a little bit beyond me. However, the accurate determination of time is a function of the observatory, and it is from its activity that we know that our time is accurate. For instance, it would be most unfortunate, Mr Chairman, if in the course of a day the clock on the wall should run ten minutes slow, and we were to work ten minutes too long. That sort of thing has to be avoided.
I think you can trust the observatory staff on that point.
The accurate determination of time is part of the work of the observatory. However, I shall endeavour to act upon my right hon. friend's suggestion.

Why is the grant made to Kingston observatory and not to others, and why is it under the Department of Transport?
I did not know the grant appeared under the Department of Transport. I would assume it has something to do with meteorology.
Perhaps the Minister of Labour could answer it.

As a member of the governing body of Queen's, the Minister of Labour might explain.

Who in the civil service is the authority on astronomy? Who sets the papers? Are they set by the civil service commission or by the department? Are the examiners men within the civil service?

I understand that it is the practice of the civil service commission, in connection with scientific and professional positions requiring certain degrees of skill, to secure expert advice as to the type of examination which should be set.
They check their academic training.

Yes. For instance, they have to certify to medical doctors. I do not know that the members of the civil service commission are qualified to pass on the technical knowledge of medical men, but they take the necessary steps to set the examination, as is done in connection with other scientific branches of the federal service.
Who marks the papers after they have tried the examination?

As I understand it, the civil service commission do not mark the papers, but they set up an examining board of experts which marks the papers or gives oral marks if the examination is oral. It is on their marking that the civil service commission finally gives its certificate.
Their report.
Their report.

I should like to say a word or two in criticism and also in support of the observatory at Ottawa. I know it is true that our observatory at Ottawa cannot compete with the great observatories of the world, but it is doing a worth while work. My only quarrel with this vote is that it is half what it should be, but I also realize that this is not the year in which to increase the item, in view of more pressing problems. I should like to point out that there is a type of astronomical observation which can be done and is being done with the equipment we have. In conjunction with other observatories, the Ottawa
Supply-Mines and Resources

observatory is doing a really worth while work which may result at some future date m the forecasting of world weather. Some very valuable research work has been done by this observatory in spectroscopy of the sun. Some humorous comments have been made on the work of astronomers, but I want to say that an astronomer is not a man who goes out, looks aloft, and writes a piece of poetry like "Twinkle, Twinkle Little Star." He is a student of a legitimate science, the forerunner of both chemistry and physics. Quite often the findings of the astronomer are communicated to the physicist and the chemist, and the result is that, for instance, we are able to make a certain type of steel in four days instead of ten. Another result was the discovery of helium by the use of which we are able to travel safely in heavier than air machines inflated by a non-inflammable gas.
Great care has been taken in years gone by to build up this observatory in Ottawa. The question has been raised if there is any collaboration between our observatory and the various astronomical departments of our universities. The answer is, yes. There is a close cohesion in this connection. Since this observatory was built some years ago it has been of real value in education. It has been pointed out that perhaps we do not need twenty-two or twenty-three astronomers, but the science of astronomy necessitates a comprehensive knowledge of mathematics and men to observe, to calculate, to chart and to analyse scientific findings. Our astronomers have been carefully educated. It has taken them years to train, and I definitely know that our astronomers in Ottawa compare favourably with those connected with other observatories in the world. The fact is that they lack the proper equipment. While our fourteen-inch telescope cannot compare with the large instrument at Victoria or the one at Mount Wilson, the fact remains that in the measurement of stellar distances, some types of spectroscopy, and in connection with research work on meteors and in the determination of the consistency of the atmosphere of the earth, valuable work has been done with so-called obsolete equipment.
If we have in mind the establishment of an air route from the Atlantic to the Pacific we must retain in this country whatever we have in the way of astrophysical, astronomical, seismographical and geodetical experts. If the finances of this countiy permit, I would suggest that next year this vote should be doubled or tripled if people are to travel safely by air from one side of this country to the other.

I notice, in the details of this item on page 119, there is a grant to the international executive council, world power conference, of $250, the same amount as the grant made last year; I assume therefore it is a recurring item. Just a word as to the world power conference. I am sure the Minister of Transport as an engineer will agree that this conference is one of the most important engineering bodies in the world. Canada is one of the most important power countries of the world. The world power conference was held in 1936, and met, I believe, in Washington. Later, the delegates had the privilege of visiting our Chippawa plant at Niagara Falls as well as other plants in Canada. The advertising alone is good for Canada. One should not underestimate from our point of view as a dominion that particular phase of the world power conference. There is also the exchange of ideas at such a meeting which is of extreme value to us. We all recognize that in certain countries of the world particularly Canada, the United States and the Scandinavian nations, water power development has been carried forward with extraordinary efficiency. The Swedes, with their new plant at Ivrongede, set a very high standard in water power development. The engineers who were responsible for the building of that government-built and government-operated plant at Krongede visited the world power conference and later came to Chippawa. I am sure our engineers received much from them and were able to give much to them in return.
We grant only $250 under this item for so important a body as the world power conference. I am sure that the minister, although he did not know there was to be another meeting of the conference in the near future, will be good enough to explain to the committee why we provide a grant of only $250 to such an important international body, and that he will also let us have his reactions, perhaps not under this grant, on the development of the international relations of Canada as one of the great power producers of the world.
That is on a per capita basis?
I do not know what is the basis of working it out, whether it is a per capita arrangement or not.
We always send a representation, do we?

I think that usually that has been done, and that when we come to consider the matter we shall probably do so again. But this $250 is simply our annual contribution to the maintenance of a permanent office in London for the countries in this conference. It is the amount that has been paid in past years, and can be regarded as Canada's share in the maintenance of that office. I assume that the United States and all the other countries which are parties to the conference also make contributions. The expense of maintaining the office between conference periods is probably not very heavy. At any rate that is our contribution and I understand that is all we have been asked for.
Whom did we send as our representative to the world power conference held in Washington in 1936?
The representative of this department at the conference a year ago was, I think, Mr. Johnston who is chief of the water and power bureau.
Did Mr. Thirpe represent the department at the world conference in 1936?

The world conference is held only every sixth year, but frequently there are sectional conferences held in intervening years. On an occasion of that kind the gentleman to whom my hon. friend refers was probably present.
