I understand the reports of the conference proceedings are printed and published and are available to people interested. The reports can be supplemented by direct information that the Canadian representative gets at the conference.

If the world power conference has any influence on the studied policy of the government, it might be well for the government to review the decisions of the conference, or the papers presented, with reference to the exchange of electric power between countries, especially the considered judgment that the exportation of power cannot be stopped without giving rise to serious international difficulty. I think if we were represented at that world conference, and if that is the considered judgment, it might be appropriate for the government during this year at least to take cognizance of the results of the last world conference.

A matter of that kind is not within the purview of the conference. The conference is held for the purpose of exchanging technical information, enabling representatives of the various countries to exchange views on power engineering science and technical matters. A conference of that kind would scarcely be concerned with questions of public policy such as that of .the export of power. According to the information supplied to me, such questions are outside the scope of the conference.

I might point out that at that conference it was indicated that in the near future all the readily available power resources of this country, the most accessible and least costly to develop, would be utilized. It was also pointed out that it is in the best interests of the dominion economically to develop industry in Canada, give employment to our own people, and stop migration to other countries. That was given, I understand, in a paper as representing Canada's views. Even though these conferences may be more or less of a technical nature-and I quite agree with the minister that I would not expect our representative at such a conference to settle or even pass much of an opinion as to the international difficulties which might arise with reference to the exchange of power between countries-I might point out that it was more or less from an engineering standpoint having regard to the amount of power available that the view was ex-
IMr. Massey.]
pressed that power should not be exported. I think it might be well at this .time for the government to review that in view of prospective developments this session.

Did I understand the minister to say in regard to this item that there are no special increases in the activities of the department this year? There is so much noise in the chamber that sometimes one can scarcely hear. Have the activities of the department been carried on about the same as previous years?
Yes.

Well, I notice the item of travelling expenses is two and one-half times greater than that for the previous year. People back home keep asking why government costs continue to increase and pile up. Can the minister explain that?

I have already explained that the amounts formerly paid directly to the department from the provinces for services rendered, have now been treated differently; the money received from the provinces now goes directly into the consolidated revenue fund, and consequent^ we have had to increase our estimates. Assessing that part of the cost against gauge readers, travelling expenses, and in other directions, accounts for the increase not only in .this particular item but in several others that have been referred to this afternoon.

I appreciate the homily that my hon. friend has directed to me, but his alarm is wholly unfounded. I have already explained, I think at least three times, that a sum of approximately $30,000, which prior to this year was received from the provincial governments for services rendered by this branch to those governments, is now paid directly into the consolidated revenue fund, and consequently we have to increase our vote to compensate for that difference. As an actual matter of fact the expenditure under this particular item this year is less than it was last year. It has not grown; it is down; but because of that method of treatment which, as I say, I have already explained to the committee several times, we have had to increase the estimate from about $197,000 to $222,000.
I wholly appreciate the importance of the point raised by the hon. member for Mount Royal. I have had a good deal of experience in the necessity of balancing budgets, others as well as my own, and I quite recognize the
importance of that. But without any offence to my hon. friend may I chide him a little bit for inconsistency. Only a short time ago on another item he suggested that we were not paying sufficiently large salaries to certain members of our staff, and that the item should be increased in order to pay larger salaries. Now he is on the other horn of the dilemma, suggesting that we should balance our budget. AVell, that is all right; but I wish to say to my hon. friend that in reality there is not an increase. There is actually a decrease.
How much of a decrease?

About $3,000 from what it was a year ago; but because of the method of treating the amounts received from the provinces for the services we render-, as compared with the treatment in other years, the item has had to be increased.

I quite appreciate the remarks of the minister. If he would take the trouble to read Hansard to-morrow he would notice that I did advocate increasing certain salaries; but I urged that the item itself should not be increased; that probably fewer could be engaged in the work, so that those retained could be paid a greater and more beneficial remuneration for their services.
What would the hon. member do with the others who were laid off?

The others would find
employment as they do now. The minister will tell the hon. member for Winnipeg North that his is a changing staff, due to the low salaries paid. These people seek employment elsewhere and take advantage of the increased remuneration that is paid in other fields. They are using the department as a place to gain experience; after that experience is obtained they go elsewhere to apply it.
I quite appreciate the fact that the minister is experiencing the difficulty of having thrown back on his department a certain decrease in revenues that formerly were obtained from the provinces; but he has had this experience, as I have, in budgeting. I have been administering and looking after a budget for the past twenty years or more, and whenever it has been found necessary to increase a budget in some respects, rather than increase the budget as a whole we have had to take away from other items in order to compensate for that greater expenditure or that loss in revenue. I think when the minister realized that the provinces were no longer going to bear this share of the cost, amounting to twenty odd thousand dollars-
Supply-Mines and Resources
May I interrupt my hon. friend? They do bear that share, but now they pay it directly into the consolidated revenue fund and not into the department.

The minister's department is not credited with it at the present time. Therefore his budget, in reference to this item, shows a noticeable increase. Rather than having to bear the responsibility for any increase, I would have taken steps to see to it that there was an appreciable decrease elsewhere to make up for that loss of revenue under this item. I am rather earnest in putting forward this plea. I am not doing it for political purposes; I do not think in my constituency it appeals one iota, because I am not interested in public works or anything of that nature. I feel, however, that to-day in Canada there is a definite sentiment-and I think the government appreciates this fact as well as I do in opposition-that government is costing us too much, not only in the dominion field but in the provincial and municipal fields as well. Sooner or later- and it might just as well be sooner-there has to be a decrease in the cost of government.
We have too many governments.

We have too many, and
those we have are too expensive. I hope next year, when these estimates are being prepared, the Minister of Finance will issue instructions to every department of government that their estimates have to come in ten per cent lower than those of the present year. Let the ministers worry as to how they are going to effect that reduction, but let him not accept any estimates which do not show that decrease. We have had to do this in other walks of life. Businesses have had to do it. Municipalities have had to do it. School boards have had to do it. We have worked under those instructions. I have had to do it. I received instructions to do it. I did not like it; but it had to be done and it was done without impairing the efficiency of the service rendered.
I want to urge that upon the minister and upon the government. It has to be done sooner or later, and I am hoping that the Minister of Finance and his colleagues who prepare these estimates will take the necessary steps to decrease the cost of government in Canada. They can decrease their own costs; they can set an example, so that other taxing bodies may do likewise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I suppose I would really be out of order in discussing on one item the general financing of the country, but I

must point out that the matter is really not quite as easy as the hon. member for Mount Royal puts it. To start with, let us consider the large items of expenditure to which he would apply the ten per cent axe to which he has refereed. For instance, let us take one of the biggest items, namely, war pensions. Obviously the reduction would not work out there. Let us consider another one, interest on debt. I am glad to be able to say, as the hon. member will find in the estimates, that there is a reduction in that item. But he would be the first to agree that that cannot be dealt with in an arbitrary manner; it is a matter of the money market, and the control of -urrency and credit.
Then, let us consider another large item- and it is in connection with the big items that the difficulty arises. We have an expenditure of $30,000,000 for old age pensions. Are we going to cut that by ten per cent? So you go through the list of uncontrollable expenditures of the government, those items which are statutory, and you will find that applying a reduction is not the same thing as applying it in an operating organization, such as a school board, a municipal organization or even a business.
There is very much less within the control of government, as such, in the Dominion of Canada than there is in any comparable organization within the country. While I appreciate the assistance of the hon. member, it would seem that so far he appears to be practically alone in his suggestions of general economy. If it was the disposition of this parliament to hold its own hand in asking for increased expenditures, that would be the most effective assistance which could be rendered to a minister of finance, in holding down the estimates, generally. For every hon. member who objects to the size of expenditure there are at least ten-often including the one who objects-who rise in their places and ask for increased expenditures along one line or another.
I am not complaining; but I say that this is a fact in parliament as it is constituted to-day, and as it has been constituted since I have had any acquaintance with it. Perhaps we could all agree that we would each take the kind of self-denying ordinance which the hon. member for Mount Royal would have me impose. It would be a great deal easier to accomplish, if all would invite it, rather than all object to its being imposed on any particular item in which they are personally or generally interested.

What percentage of national
expenditures are controllable, and what percentage uncontrollable?
FEBRUARY 22, 193S	699
Supply-Mines and Resources

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot answer offhand.
Approximately.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would not attempt to
state it even approximately. We might differ as to definitions. If we take as uncontrollable only that which is statutory, then of course we would reach a conclusion different from that which we must reach if we examined each expenditure, and decided for ourselves as to whether it was or was not controllable. However, I shall have that information later in the session. I have not an answer at the present time, and I do not wish to make a guess.

I do not want the minister
to feel that I am not fully cognizant of the difficulties a minister of finance or a minister of natural resources must face. I quite appreciate what has been said. I am sorry if I am wandering away from the item under discussion; but let me point out that last year under the item of conversions we saved S6.000.000. What was done with it? That $6,000,000 was gobbled up, along with about $20,000,000 more.
The military estimates.

That money is gone. If
we could only have held the estimates at what they were last year we would have accomplished something. That is the point I am trying to make. Hold them; keep them fixed. On the same page on which appears the item we are discussing, there is another one which involves a tremendous increase.
No, no.

Oh, I know that supposedly
there is a decrease.
It is an actual decrease.

But if you show it to the
ordinary citizen he will say there is an increase, because the figures are there. I know the reason for it; but if you take the aggregate of the figures to be presented by the Minister of Mines and Resources, I dare say those estimates will show an increase, not a decrease. Surely to goodness we can draw the line and say, "They are fixed; they cannot go higher than that." Then when we make conversions and save $6,000,000; when the pensions decrease as, over a period of years, they will, and as other fixed items show a decrease, we can gradually bring the estimates down to a more reasonable basis. That is the point I make.
I am not unappreciative of the difficulties of this or any other department of government, but I feel it is time to call a halt to government expenditures, particularly if they seem to be excessive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member will take the estimates on his desk and look at page 2, he will find a summary of the totals of all departments, showing the increase or decrease as compared with the main estimates for the current year. At the bottom of the page he will see that the aggregate amount of the main estimates now under consideration is $2,900,471.65 less than the aggregate of the main estimates for the current year. Of course that does not tell the whole story. Everything depends upon what will be added, in due course, as a result of supplementary estimates. But I must repeat that the comparison between the main estimates now presented and the main estimates presented last session is favourable to the amount I have indicated. I believe this is a reasonably fair comparison of departmental and running expenses of government in one year as compared with those in another. On that page the decreases or increases are shown, department by department, and the result, as I have indicated, is an aggregate decrease of $2,900,471.65.
That is not the general impression in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But that is the truth.

The impression conveyed through the editorial columns of newspapers is that there is an actual increase in the estimates before us to-day as compared with the estimates brought down on a similar occasion last year. It is indicated that there is an increase of between S20,000,000 and $30,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know where the hon. member gets that information.
Well, I have the information. I would like to look it up and bring it to the chamber later.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am giving only the facts.

In connection with the items respecting the dominion water and power bureau, with which we are now dealing, I say that the new system of accounting is not satisfactory. If, for instance, Ontario owed an amount for work done by the bureau, the latter should get credit for it. In the same way, that credit should be shown so that hon. members may know what is going on. We should know about the work done for the different provinces. For instance, how do I know how much has been done in Saskatche-
Supply-Mines and Resources

wan in the past year? I should know that, and I should know what work is done by the department in every part of Canada. We should know about departmental affairs. If we are at all interested, we should gain a more general knowledge.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member's
problem is that of knowing where to look for the information. I shall be very glad to tell him. The principle upon which the revenues of Canada have been operated for many years is laid down in the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. The basic principle is that all moneys shall go into one consolidated fund. There was the odd departure, such as occurred in this particular department, where the moneys were collected and disbursed by the branch. I think the hon. member will agree that that would not be a good business principle to adopt in running the affairs of the country.
The fact that moneys are collected by the department for services rendered is of record. There should be no difficulty about the matter as the auditor general's report which I tabled a week or two ago contains not only the particulars of the expenditures of each department but the particulars of the revenues received. The point raised by the minister in connection with this matter is that we have recently applied the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act to the revenues collected by this branch. Formerly this was not the case. On every occasion on which the auditor general learns that there is any revenue collected by a department and retained and expended by that department, my attention is called to the procedure and it is stopped. Such money goes into the consolidated revenue fund and the expenditures of each department must be voted by this house out of the consolidated revenue fund of the country.
Will there be anything in the supplementary estimates for this item?
I cannot say definitely, but I think it is unlikely.

The minister has said that there is a reduction in these items, and in order to see whether that is the case it would be necessary to know whether anything will be included in the supplementary estimates.
I do not anticipate that there will be any increase in this particular vote.

Item agreed to.

Lake of the Woods control board, $7,576.
Do the United States pay an amount equal to this vote?

They pay an amount
based upon their particular interest in this lake. The larger part of the Lake of the Woods lies within Canada, a small area being in the United States.

The northwest angle
and all the water immediately south would be in United States territory.

I think there is one bay at the end of the lake which is in the United States, but I cannot give its relative proportion to the whole lake. I should say that perhaps three-quarters of the lake is in Canadian territory.
What is the purpose of this control?

The purpose is to regulate the flow of water from the lake into the AVinnipeg river by maintaining the lake level between certain datum points, I think between 1059 and 1064. It is essential that the flow of water into the Winnipeg river should be controlled in order that the power plants located on the river may operate at the proper capacity.
Is the total cost of this control paid by the federal government, or does Manitoba contribute?
An agreement has been entered into by Manitoba and Ontario with the federal government covering the division of expenses. The two provinces contribute to these expenses.
Has this control board given satisfaction since its establishment in the control of the waters of the Winnipeg river?
I think it has given general satisfaction. At any rate, since I have had anything to do with this department no complaints have been received.
How many outlets are there to the lake?
I think there is only one, the Winnipeg river at the north.

Item agreed to.
To provide for the expenses incurred under the agreement between the dominion, Ontario and Manitoba confirmed by the Lac Seul Conservation Act, 1928, money expended to be reimbursed, $20,000.

Just what does this control consist of, and does it cover control over the waters between lake St. Joseph and Lac Seul?

Supply-Mines and Resources

I do not think lake St. Joseph is involved in this particular control. Lac Seul lies wholly within the province of Ontario and it drains into the Winnipeg river. The regulation of the flow of water from Lac Seul to the Winnipeg river is an important factor in the maintenance of sufficient water in the river to enable the power plants to operate at the proper capacity. There is also a power site, on the English river, that drains Lac Seul into the Winnipeg river, and the control of these waters will also be important when that power site is developed, as it probably will be at some future date. The expenditure in connection with the regulation of the flow of water from the lake is actually borne by the provincial governments.

Item agreed to.
Engineering and construction service, $136,190.
Mr. MASSEY': Is this the item under which I should discuss the possible development of iron mining in the northwest territories and within the arctic circle? I desire to be in order as I do not want to mislead again the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Finn).
That discussion would come properly under item No. 125, or any of the other items under the mines and geology branch.
The minister would rather that I did not discuss it under this item?
I think it is advisable to keep within the item before the committee.
What is covered by this item?

That covers the expenses of this branch in connection with engineering sendees for the whole department. The national parks, which are administered by the Department of Mines and Resources, contain about 900 miles of roads and in addition to that the department is constructing the highway from Banff to Jasper. It is also constructing the section of the trans-Canada highway between Golden and Revelstoke. That was an obligation first undertaken by the government of the present Prime Minister when he was formerly at the head of the government, and was later added to by the present leader of the opposition in 1933 or 1934. Then there are a few architects in connection with designing buildings in the parks, and Indian schools and Indian office buildings that have to be erected here and there for administrative purposes. That and the clerks and draftsmen comprise the greater part of the expense. Of
this amount of $136,000 odd. approximately $119,000 or $120,000 is for salaries. There is .$6,000 for printing and stationery, provision for drafting blue-prints and plans, and so on, travelling expenses and sundry items.
This is what one might call the design and supervision-to take one instance-of the Banff-Jasper highway?
Yes.
Where is the vote for the actual work that is being carried out?
Part of the expenditures in connection with the Banff-Jasper and the Revelstoke-Golden roads is included in this; that is, the supervision of the staff that is doing the work.

What about wages,
dynamite and tools?
That is not in this.
Where is it?

That will be in the
supplementary vote when brought down. It is hoped to carry on the work this year.
Is it still looked upon as a relief measure?

I think it will probably be voted in the supplementary estimates this year. Since 1931 or 1932 that work has been more or less classed as relief work. It has been carried on under the former Public Works Construction Act, and later special supplementary estimates were introduced. In the public mind it is related to relief. The likelihood is that when the votes for these works are brought down this year they will be brought down as straight supplementary estimates.

Item agreed to.
Geodetic service, $160,500.
WThat is the reason for the increase in this item?

It is all accounted for by the five per cent salary deduction that was restored a year ago. The estimates brought down at that time did not include the five per cent increase; it is included in the present estimates. I believe that actually, if we put it on a proper comparative basis, there would be a slight decline in the vote.

Why does an item
sometimes refer to temporary assistance, whereas this one speaks of wages? Is there any relation between the two? The wages item is up $4,000.
Supply-Mines and Resources
The wages here are for the field parties that go out on geodetic surveys. This item of wages is to cover the help that is required, I suppose, such as canoe men, cooks, labourers and the like.
Will there be a greater number of parties out this year to account for the fifty per cent increase in wages?
No. There will be no more parties out this year than last year: probably not so many.
Then why is the item up $4,000?
The increase is partly accounted for by the restoration of the five per cent cut.
Oh, no. It was $9,700 and it is now $13,600.
It is a separate item.

There has been a decrease in certain other items that go to make up the total vote, and that decrease has been used up, so to speak, in an endeavour to increase the field work, which has fallen behind to some extent.
There is an increase in travelling expenses. Does this mean that there are more people travelling, or are we to assume that they pay more and have better accommodation?

There is an increase from $950 to $1,350, or an increase of $400. That is put there because in the program of work this year the engineers will probably have to go a little further from Ottawa than they did a year ago. The work will be in the lower St. Lawrence, and some part of it in British Columbia.

Item agreed to.
International boundary commission, $30,800.

What relation has the work performed by the engineers referred to in this particular item to the work which, the minister said, engineers had to do in relation to international waters under item No. 152? Further, Canada votes $30,800 this year for the international boundary commission; do the United States vote an equal amount, and do the United States estimates call for the same number of engineers, namely five?

As a matter of fact the United States spend a very considerable amount more on this work than Canada does. The international boundary commission have the responsibility of maintaining the bound-

ary markings between Canada and the United States. That work, of course, has to be carefully and accurately done. I understand that periodically they cover the boundary, see that the markings are maintained, that is, that the posts are in place, and if the line runs through an area where there is timber it is cut out for a certain distance on either side. For the past few years they have been working accurately to define the boundary in the mountain section in British Columbia between that province and the states on the south. That is substantially the routine work of the commission.

Here again we have this division of items into a thing called "wages," which is $1,200 up, and then total salaries and wages, which is $2,000 up. What is this item of "wages" which is continually appearing?

That, again, covers the labourers and help of that kind which is necessary on these survey parties. For instance they send out a party to mark these boundaries; they require equipment and labourers if a boundary line passes through timber which has grown up and has to be cut out and cleared up. The item covers expenses incidental to that class of work.

The minister stated that the five per cent was applicable to the last item. I see from the details that the salaries of the engineer, surveys engineers, etc., to the international boundary commission are exactly the same as they were a year ago. Would that five per cent increase not apply to them?

If the hon. member will look at page 121 he will see that the vote was precisely the same a year ago as it is this year, but the $978 which was the salary deduction of five per cent was taken off last year; it is not taken off this year.
Is the work of this commission about completed? From year to year we have heard it was almost done and that we might hope to have it finished at any time, except for maintenance.

The work is now, I believe, very largely maintenance work. I am informed that there are still a few sections of boundary, practically all in the more northern regions between Alaska and Canada, to be definitely determined. But the vote is practically all a maintenance work vote. It is necessary to have the boundary markings properly placed and maintained.

Item agreed to.

Copyright Amendment Act
Hydrographic and map service-hydrographic service, $418,000.

In connection with this item the same point again arises; we have $75,000 for wages and another amount for temporary help, bringing the total for wages and temporary help up to $109,000. How are these temporary employees engaged and how is the help recruited which is classed under the item "wages"? Approximately one-fourth of the whole item is either temporary help under its own classification or under the classification of "wages." There are many unemployed in my riding, and if the department would take temporary employees on a basis of so many from each riding, there are a number of men in my district who might qualify for this temporary employment. How are they engaged and from where do they come?

I am informed that to carry on this work four or five boats are in use during the period that the survey work is proceeding. It is necessary to have officers and crews, and according to the information given me, the item in the explanatory notes for temporary assistance covers ship's officers and temporary staff. If the hon. member will refer to page 122 of the estimates he will see that the item of $34,000 odd compares with $29,000 odd a year ago. Probably-I do not know-it is planned in the department to carry the work on for a little longer than it was carried on a year ago. The same explanation would apply to wages.

But how are these
temporary employees and wage earners engaged?

Temporary employees are certified by the civil service commission. The ordinary labourers, as I believe always has been the case, are not.
Progress reported.

maintopic: COPYRIGHT AMENDMENT 'ACT, 1931   FURNISHING OF LIST OF DRAMATICO-MUSICAL OR MUSICAL WORKS OWNED OR CONTROLLED   PUBLIC RADIO RECEPTION OR GRAMOPHONE REPRODUCTION

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, February 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Esling for the second reading of Bill No. 12, to amend the Copyright Amendment Act, 1931.

maintopic: COPYRIGHT AMENDMENT 'ACT, 1931   FURNISHING OF LIST OF DRAMATICO-MUSICAL OR MUSICAL WORKS OWNED OR CONTROLLED   PUBLIC RADIO RECEPTION OR GRAMOPHONE REPRODUCTION
speechtext:
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) upon his initiative in introducing this bill, and upon his tenacity of purpose in pursuing the object of this bill session after session. This bill, as I understand it, merely requires the Canadian Performing Right Society to publish a list of the musical compositions which they purport to control, under the provisions of the Copyright Act; and, second, to exempt from payment of the fee provided under the terms of the act small business establishments which use the radio in a limited way. The Canadian Performing Right Society is a monopoly, a monopoly which in the exercise of its rights has incurred the antipathy and antagonism of countless people all the way across this country. This monopoly claims to have and to control the performing rights in the repertoires of the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers, the Performing Right Society, Limited, of England, and the societies of France, Germany, Austria, Italy, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, Hungary, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Roumania, Portugal. Switzerland, Brazil, Belgium and Holland, and it maintains that included in its repertoire are some two million pieces of music. In order to impress upon its prospective customers the necessity of taking out a licence and complying with its requirements, and paying the fees which it exacts, it sends out a circular letter which contains this paragraph:
In order that the society's legal rights in the performance of the copyright music which it controls may be appreciated, we beg to draw your attention to the recent actions in court taken by the society against (1) La Paloma Restaurant Limited of 38C Yonge street, Toronto, Ontario, and (2) Champs Hotel & Cafe Limited of 1905 South Railway street, Regina, Saskatchewan.
Copyright Amendment Act

The society gives those two illustrations to show the extent of its influence and that it intends to enforce the rights which it claims from one end of the country to the other.
I am fully in accord with the generally accepted legal principle that a vendor must establish a good title to that which he proposes to sell. This society carries on its activities by means of spotters and agents who are located in the principal cities of the dominion and who travel from place to place. People who have radios in their places of business have no knowledge that these spotters or agents are among their customers. These spottera and agents visit fraternal societies where concert performances are put on, and should any musical number be included in the performance that fraternal society receives a demand either from the Performing Right Society itself or from its solicitors.
There is in progress at the present time in Regina a lawsuit in which this society seeks an injunction to restrain a small restaurant from receiving through the medium of its radio, for which it has paid the regular licence fee, a certain piece of music. Not long ago a restaurant proprietor received a demand from this society setting out that during a certain hour at his place of business there was received over the radio certain pieces of music, including "Mr. Ghost Goes to Town." The proprietor of that restaurant did not know that the Canadian Performing Right Society was included among his customers. The next piece was entitled, "You are all I Need." I assume they meant by that that his custom was what the society required. Should he comply with their requirement, sign an application for a licence, give the details which they require from time to time and pay the fee, the next number received in his place of business would be entirely applicable, being entitled "You're an Angel." And if he continued paying these fees and filing the returns required by the society from time to time, the title of the next piece of music would be most appropriate: "When I grow too old to Dream." He and his customers having listened to these selections of music, he was required to take out a licence, to send in the details which they require from time to time and to pay a minimum licence fee of $10. Bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the proprietor of this and proprietors of hundreds of other establishments have paid the regular licence fee required by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, for the use of a radio receiving set, and having paid that fee and made his

investment in the radio he feels he is entitled to receive over the air the broadcast programs.

Shortly after the radio was installed in the rotunda, he W'as called on by a representative of this organization who was described to me as both ignorant and insolent. Copyright Amendment Act
That is not unreasonable at all. Other organizations, such as churches, service clubs, etc., put on numbers without knowing that this society holds any copyright on them, and then they are called upon and required to pay a fee. The Saskatchewan Hotels Association, at a recent meeting, passed a resolution authorizing the president to write a letter in this regard, and I assume that letter has been received by many hon. members. In any case, a day or so ago I received such a letter, dated Regina, February 10,	1938.

We all remember that the bill which was presented to this house last year was well received, and that it was not passed just because we were asked to test for another year the act in force. It did not get through because the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) asked us to leave the question in abeyance for another twelve months. Secretary of State whether circumstances now permit to grant the hon. member's request and to agree to the amendments which he is proposing. Copyright Amendment Act

to section 10 of the Copyright Amendment Act, 1931, reads as follows; from the 20th line down:
. . . and with each application for a licence or for the renewal thereof, the society shall furnish to those from whom fees are to be collected in compensation for the use of music on which the society controls copyright, a list of all titles of dramatico-musical or musical works so owned or controlled. Such list shall give the title, the name of the author and the date on which and country in which the %vork was copyrighted and the date on -which the society registered in the Copyright Office at Ottawa its ownership or control of such work, and such list shall be certified to by the Secretary of State as a correct list of the works so registered.

A hotelkeeper of Jacques Cartier constituency, which I have the honour to represent, brought to my attention a case which is typical of the procedure of this company's employees. Two customers entered his hotel and ordered a drink. After listening to the music provided by a special instrument installed in the hotel, they requested that a certain composition be played. When the hotelkeeper placed the record in the instrument and set it in motion, they informed him that he would have to pay a licence fee of S30 to the Canadian Performing Right Society Limited. From the speeches which we have just heard, it would seem that all are desirous of supporting this bill and I am sure we can ask the honourable the Secretary of State if circumstances have changed since last year, and if the general conditions connected with this matter have shown any improvement. Mr. Speaker, I cannot help feeling that the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) is in the right vibration when in this bill he attempts to contest the position of the Canadian Performing Right Society. It is absolutely necessary that we in Canada benefit by the cultural heritage and achievements of the world in general, and it is not unjust that when these things lie outside the public domain we should be prepared to pay for the use of them.
I am disposed to believe that the performing right society, in dispensing their wares to the people of Canada, are assuming all the prerogatives of a complete monopoly, and they are doing this in the not unnatural assurance that time will tend to confirm them in their position, and to eliminate contending elements. I am disposed to believe that they are quite unable to produce a list of the works which they assume to control. I have in mind the facility with which such a society can procure the services of hacks in order to make arrangements of certain works which lie in the public domain, or of which they would not be able to avail themselves in their original presentation.
Having said this, I reach the matter of broadcasting. I contend that the Canadian Performing Right Society has no right to assert itself beyond the original broadcasting studio. The government licenses radios through its own company, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and pays for the programs it broadcasts. In such a transaction with the society there should begin and end the expression of the society's position. To-day the society collects at the point of broadcast, and then it follows the waves along to collect again at the point of dissemination. In my opinion, in so doing it invades a territory to which it has no title, and usurps a function to which it has no right. Further, I believe its activity in any country, and especially in Canada under present conditions, will tend to destroy the development of cultural initiative upon the part of our people. If it is left secure in its monopolistic arrogance, small inducement will be presented to Canadian artists to produce Canadian works. The more I think of the matter the more I am satisfied that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is the one company representing this cultural arm of the government and the people of Canada, and that it should deal with all users of radio, and with broadcasting media.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should contract with the performing right society, and with any other group of cultural 51952-451
disseminators-there is no reason to believe there will not be others-in arranging reasonable tax rates which may be recovered through small added taxes on restaurants, hotels or other disseminating users. Such taxes should also provide an excess which would be applied to recompense purely Canadian talent in Canada, and so bring us to the honoured place where we might receive and rejoice in a greatly increased Canadian cultural expression. while still paying reasonable tribute tor what the world has to give us.
For these reasons I have much pleasure in supporting the bill.

maintopic: COPYRIGHT AMENDMENT 'ACT, 1931   FURNISHING OF LIST OF DRAMATICO-MUSICAL OR MUSICAL WORKS OWNED OR CONTROLLED   PUBLIC RADIO RECEPTION OR GRAMOPHONE REPRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling), has expressed the hope that in considering this bill hon. members will look upon it not as a party matter but simply as a means of serving their constituents. I believe the hon. member will admit that that hope has been largely fulfilled inasmuch as the expressions of opinion have not been along party lines. Hon. members have expressed their individual opinions when speaking to this bill. As a general rule this is how copyright matters have been treated when brought before the house. Before I became a member of the government I remember that hon. members on both sides treated this involved and complex matter of copyright as one of individual concern.
Before I discuss the bill itself I should like to enunciate one or two principles which, it seems to me, must be considered in a discussion of this bill. Whether or not the bill is adopted, I do not think its meaning should be misconstrued. Copyright is by no means a tax or a permit or a levy; it is a property right. If a man has written a book or composed a piece of music, not only is he entitled to be considered the author or composer; not only is he entitled to the profits from the sales of such book or music, but he has the right to control over the performance thereof. In my opinion we should not tamper with this sacred principle.
I might add that in considering this bill we are dealing not with the principle of copyright, but with the Canadian Performing Right Society which claims to have acquired the performing rights to not only one, to not only a hundred, but to a million pieces of music. We have to face not just the exercise of a right by an author or composer, but the exercise of rights by a monopoly covering the performance of practically all music subject to copyright. I am sure that
Copyright Amendment Act

the introducer of this bill will not object to this distinction, as I think it gives to his bill the strength he is seeking.
Different governments that have had to do with copyright have taken the stand that there should be sections in the bill dealing with societies such as the one we are discussing. Following the international conference which took place in Rome in 1928, the Secretary of State of that time introduced a bill in 1931. While that bill followed fairly closely what had been adopted in Rome, the then Secretary of State felt that there should be a special section dealing with societies such as the Canadian Performing Right Society and section 10 of the amending bill of 1931 deals with that situation.
Subsection 2 of that section states that whenever in the opinion of the minister a society controlling a large number of pieces files rates that seem to be excessive, it shall be within the power of the minister to institute an inquiry into such rates. After representations had been made to the then government, the then Secretary of State took the stand that the rates of the Canadian Performing Right Society were disputable. Under an order in council dated March 22, 1935, the then government appointed Judge Parker as a commissioner to inquire into the Canadian Performing Right Society. This inquiry has been alluded to in former debates, and time will not permit me to go into any detail. The commissioner went into the situation very thoroughly and filed a report dated October 29, 1935.
It then became the duty of the succeeding government, through myself as Secretary of State, to give consequence to that report. I think the amending bill of 1935 implemented all the recommendations contained in the report, the main one being the appointment of an appeal board before which the rates of societies such as the one we are discussing could be considered by both sides. The decision of the board was to be final. When my hon. friend introduced his bill last year, I pointed out that this appeal board had been in existence for only a couple of months and it did not seem fair to amend the act further without waiting to see how the board worked out.
I pointed out also that it was the hope of the government that an international conference might be held in Brussels at which copyright matters would be considered. For these reasons it did not seem to me advisable to further amend the act. The house rejected that bill; but, as has been stated to-night,

this rejection was not because of the principle of the bill but because the house was willing to agree with my argument for delay.
This appeal board has now sat on two different occasions, once in December, 1936, and again in December, 1937. I have come to the conclusion that as regards the first section of this bill, it is not within the competence of the board at all and it is not likely that we shall get any enlightenment from that source. In connection with the matter dealt with by the second section, that is, the rates charged by the performing right society to hotels, restaurants and other places where music is reproduced by a mechanical process, the board apparently has taken the stand that it must maintain some rates as long as the act acknowledges the right to charge a certain rate for a certain purpose. I agree that the house must now deal with this bill on its merits. The reasons that actuated me in asking the house last year not to hurry into a pronouncement on the bill do not exist at the present time.
As for the international conference, I regret to say that it seems to have been indefinitely postponed. By that, I do not mean that it may be years before a meeting of the kind is held, but the fact is that no positive date is actually foreseen. That may be due perhaps to the grave international difficulties which exist abroad. I think, however, that it would be a mistake, if an adjustment must be made, to delay the matter further merely in the hope that perhaps within a certain space of time we may have more definite pronouncements on these very questions.
Of course, the main difficulty that parliament cannot escape is the question whether we can adopt a bill of this kind without contravening the agreement which we have entered into with the other nations. That, I must admit, is a most embarrassing question, and I must say that, so far as authorities are concerned. I have not been able to secure any agreement in that respect. It would not be fair to the house if I did not say that there may be a doubt as to whether, according to the Rome agreement of 1928, we can do exactly what my hon. friend proposes to-night. But the doubt is just as grave in the other direction. It can be contended, though, that the meeting of 1928, as regards a monopolistic society such as the one we are now discussing, made no definite pronouncement. I know that in several countries since that conference there has been adopted some method of control, either state control or control through an appeal board such as wc have in Canada, or control by means of legislation of some kind.

Copyright Amendment Act
I do not think I am misleading the house when I say that the question of control over a very large number of copyright pieces, such as is claimed by the performing right society, could not fail to be one of the main features of a future international conference and agreement; but I cannot say that we have any definite pronouncement to the effect that that would preclude parliament from adopting measures of control in face of a situation of that kind.
That would apply especially to the first section wherein it is proposed that the company shall furnish to those to whom they sell licences, lists of works for which they claim copyright and performing right. I must say in all frankness that I consider the section rather futile; I do not think it is very useful. If you consider it carefully you will find that this society in selling licences allows the use of everything it has in stock. There is no reason, therefore, why anybody buying a licence should desire to have a list of all the works controlled by the society, because he knows when he buys a licence that he is free to use any. The section will be more useful when in the future several societies control different lists and appear on the market; but at the present time I do not think the section can be very useful, and I know it would be burdensome to the society and might have the effect in the long run of forcing them with a certain degree of reasonableness, to increase the price of their licence. But as we have provided in previous legislation to exact from the society a list to be filed with the Secretary of State, I fail to see, although the argument has been presented to us from outside quarters, how there can be more of a contravention of any international agreement to provide that, such a list having been filed with us, it should also be supplied to the public. For that reason I shall not take exception to the section, although, as I have said, I do not think it will serve any great purpose.
The second section is in my opinion much more important. It deals with the reproduction of music, by radio or gramophone. This was one of the principal subjects discussed at the last conference in Rome, and it was dealt with in two articles which I shall put on Hansard:
Article 11 bis.
(1)	The authors of literary and artistic works enjoy the exclusive right to authorize the communication of their works to the public by radio diffusion.
(2)	It belongs to the national legislatures of the countries of the union to regulate the conditions for the exercise of the right declared in the preceding paragraph, but such conditions
shall have an effect strictly limited to the country which establishes them. They cannot in any case adversely affect the moral right of the author, nor the right which belongs to the author of obtaining an equitable remuneration fixed, in default of an amicable agreement, by competent authority.
Article 13.
(1)	Authors of musical works have the exclusive right to authorize: (1) the adaptation of these works to instruments serving to reproduce them mechanically; (2) the public performance of the same works by means of these instruments.
(2)	The limitations and conditions relative to the application of this article shall be determined by the domestic legislation of each country in its own case; but all limitations and conditions of this nature shall have an effect strictly limited to the country which shall have adopted them.
If you interpret these two articles in the only way in which they can be interpreted, there is no doubt in the first place that the composer of music is entitled to performing right when his music is reproduced by any mechanical process. But there is no doubt, either, that the convention has left to the individual countries which are parties to the agreement the right to legislate upon the matter in the way they think best suited to their own requirements. In 1931-and I must hasten, because I should like to get through before nine o'clock-the Secretary of State of the time in dealing with these articles added to his act a paragraph in the definitions reading:
(q) "performance" means any acoustic representation of a work or any visual representation of any dramatic action in a work, including a representation made by means of any mechanical instrument or by radio communication.
I submit that by the articles which I have read and also by this definition, which is included in our act, it is clearly stipulated that something should be paid for the performance by mechanical process of any piece of music. But it stops there. There has been no further provision preventing the government from legislating as to the price of the performance being paid one way or the other.
Let me now deal with the radio situation- and I think I can do so in very few words. The broadcasting stations are already paying to the Canadian Performing Right Society a very considerable price for the broadcasting of music. I am quite willing to take the stand personally that this is the proper way to meet the situation, because the broadcasting station chooses the piece of music that it wants to broadcast; it picks one piece of music rather than another. That is the very spirit of copyright; if you want to play my music you must pay me for it; if not, then do not play it. But what about the poor
Copyright Amendment Act

fellow in the small restaurant who has a radio and turns it on to get a hockey match or, it may be, a speech by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). It may be a dramatic representation. And if, perchance, after one has listened to those different broadcasts for fifteen minutes-

Was the Lillooet in commission last year?

No; she is laid up and
will not be used this year, I am told.

Is there not ample need
for both boats operating on the Pacific coast?

There are two; there is
the Pender and the William J. Stewart.
The Pender is only a houseboat, is it not?

No; it is a little bigger
than a houseboat; it does good work. The William J. Stewart of course, is the large boat of the service.

Item agreed to.
Legal surveys and map service, including grant of $350 to assist in printing the publication of the Canadian Institute of Surveying, $171,510.

How many people in
the public service are engaged in making maps?

I am afraid I cannot at
the moment give information as to the total number. In this particular subdivision of the department there are sixty-four permanent employees.

Perhaps the minister
will say what other departments are engaged in making maps.

The
Department of National Defence for one.

That and the Department
of Mines and Resources I think are the only two.
I think the minister will find that there is another. Who makes the maps connected with the franchise act?
That is done under this particular vote.
They are doing that now?

Yes; that is part of the work which comes under this vote. I might
Supply-Mines and Resources

give the functions of the staff engaged under this vote. They are: To undertake all legal surveys required by the Department of Mines and Resources, including the Northwest and Yukon territories, National paries, ordnance lands and Indian reserves, and the legal surveys required by other government departments; to maintain the central office for indexing, filing and recording survey returns and plans of the surveys and engineering branch and supplying information from them; to compile and prepare from existing base maps or from published maps, electoral maps and general maps for use of the various government departments, air navigation maps, natural resource and railway maps, general maps of Canada and all types of maps except topographic made from original field surveys; and to print maps and charts, to distribute all departmental maps except those relating to mines and geology. Roughly those are the functions which are carried on by the subdivision covered by this vote.
May I ask the minister why there is such a large increase, amounting to approximately S10,000, in the provision for temporary service in this branch of his department?

I am informed by the director that certain maps had to be prepared in connection with the trans-Canada air service and that there are temporary employees engaged for that work, which, I take it, largely accounts for the increase in temporary assistance from S1.980 to $12,010.
But these estimates become effective only on the first day of April next.
That is what it is for.
It cannot be for past expenditure.
I am informed that they have started the work already. I do not know how they are being paid at the moment.
There is a prohibition against it in the statute.
I certainly hope we are not violating any statute.

The minister knows that the statement made to him a moment ago by the director could not be possible within the law; that is, this could not be for work which has already commenced. These estimates have no applicability to anything until the first day of April, 1938, unless we vote money for governor general's warrants or matters of that kind. If this work is undertaken to be paid for out of a vote to be

made, it is against the statute in that case made and provided, under which there must be an appropriation before the work can be undertaken unless there is a governor general'6 warrant for it.
From the information I get from the director I think perhaps the Department of Transport advanced a certain amount of money.
Out of unforeseen expenses, probably.
Probably; I do not know out of what vote it comes, but it is from that money that the staff presently engaged are being paid.
The trans-Canada airways is a separate entity, and there was provision with respect to its capital being advanced to pay for services rendered by the government. That might be the position.
That may be the position.

In connection with all these items which refer to temporary assistance and wages the hon. member for Lincoln made the statement earlier in the day that the total was approximately half a million dollars. I have not made the total to be much over $100,000, but that is a good deal of money. In reference to what the minister said earlier in the afternoon, namely that the civil service commission selects those who are to perform the temporary service, I should like to ask a further question. If that is the case, there must have been a tremendous number of jobs advertised by the civil service commission. I have seen some jobs advertised, but nothing like the number that this provision for temporary service would call for. So I ask the minister: Are jobs which come under the heading of temporaiy assistance advertised and the successful applicants selected by the civil service commission?

Yes; but I might point out to my hon. friend that the temporary assistance referred to here might refer to civil servants who have been temporary for eight or ten years. That is, the employees have been in the service under a temporary classification and not in the permanent service.
That avoids superannuation difficulties.
Yes. As a matter of fact, I think there is a margin maintained in all the departments.

I believe there is a regulation covering the permanent and temporaiy employees in all the departments.

Supply-National Defence
It is eighty to twenty, I believe.

To what extent has the public supported this mapmaking service? To what extent does the public purchase the maps, either by single copies, by the hundred or by the thousand, for use of societies and so on?

I am informed that we get about eighty or ninety orders a day for maps, and a small charge is made. Personally I think a charge should be made for every map which goes out, and, for that matter, for most reports which go out from government departments as well. Probably it would curb a little the demand that comes from certain quarters for maps and government reports of one kind and another. I think the principle is sound, and I may say here that it is one the application of which we hope to extend in this department.
Has the minister any figures as to the revenue over the last few years? Is it increasing?
I am informed that from the distribution of maps we receive between $8,000 and $9,000 a year.
Item agreed to.
General-Book of Remembrance, $10,000.
Would the minister tell us just what progress has been made with the book of remembrance?

speakeroldname: Hon. IAN MACKENZIE (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
The agreement, approved by order in council, P.C. 865, of April 23, 1937, entered into with James Purves, heraldic artist, illuminator and designer, for the executing and completion of the book of remembrance expires on March 31, 1939. The hon. gentleman said 1937.

Will copies of this book be made for distribution or sale to the public?

Those will be photographic copies, as I understand it?
Yes, and a reproduction copy will be available.
