Departmental administration, $190,070.

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this covers the
administration of the offices of the Minister of Public Works, the deputy minister, the purchasing agent, and the secretary of the department. The increase of $12,000 is mostly accounted for by the restoration of the five per cent cut, and statutory increases and promotions in the department. There are just a few new appointments.
Just a few? .
Not very many

I should like to ask a question, but if this is not the proper time I shall not go ahead with it. I should like to learn from the minister the routine between the Department of Public Works and the Post Office Department with reference to the moving of a post office from one situation to another. I have in mind something about which I wired the minister just before leaving for the coronation, namely the removal of a post office on St. Clair avenue west, Toronto, from ward 6 to ward 5. The information I
Supply-Public Works

got at that time was that it was on recommendation from the Post Office Department to the Department of Public Works that the work was being done. Is this the proper time to ask the question? Is this the item under which an order for the removal of a post office from one position to another may be discussed?
The patronage committee, I would think.

Generally speaking, we
follow the recommendation of the Post Office Department when they contend that the space allotted to them is not sufficient, or the building is not a proper one. Of course that is a general statement, but we must remember that the case mentioned by the hon. member is also very general. If he would give me further detail, I should be only too happy to give him all the information he wishes when we are considering the estimates at a later date. Probably he will indicate to me the special case he has in mind.
Would the minister explain the provision of 83,000 for travelling expenses?

That amount covers the travelling expenses of the officers of the main office in Ottawa, including the deputy minister, the assistant to the deputy minister, and other officers of the branch headed by the minister. As I said a minute ago, the item covers the minister's office, and those of the deputy minister, the assistant deputy minister, the purchasing agent and the secretary of the department. It happens that the officers of these different branches have to travel, and that item covers it. I regret I have not the full particulars, but I shall have them later on. My idea was simply to call an item in the department.
So we may take it to mean that in addition to this amount, there are other travelling expenses in the department.

Yes; for example, there are travelling expenses in the architects' branch, the chief engineer's branch, the telegraph branch, and others. These travelling expenses are enumerated under the different items, and when we reach them we will give the details. As I pointed out earlier, these travelling expenses relate more particularly to the offices of the minister and the deputy minister.

In the item I notice
what would appear to be a departure from or innovation in the practice of the department. So far as I know, for the first time there appears in the estimates an item of

S3.300, for a clerk of tenders. I had not known of any such official in that department in the past, and I should like to know if this is a new departure. If so, what reasons have prompted the change? I know the minister appreciates the importance of this matter. A great many tenders are invited by the Department of Public Works, through advertising. The tenders come in sealed. In the past they have been left in the custody of the secretary, the deputy minister or some other official of the department. When (he time arrived for the opening of tenders, those who had tendered were invited, and had a right to be present when the tenders were opened. I know that was true in the last few years, and I assume it is a practice which has continued under the present ministry.
Formerly there was no clerk of tenders, and I am wondering why it is thought necessary at this time to make the appointment, and to set up a new office. To cover the whole matter, and to save time when he is answering, the minister might tell us whether the clerk of tenders is a new appointee, whether he is appointed by the civil service commission, whether he was in the employ of the department before, and who he is.

I regret that at this time, for the reasons I have set out, I am not in a position to give the hon. member all these details. The position is new, but the man occupying it is a former employee of the department. He was in the service, and this is just a change of title which has been given to a man already in the service. If my memory serves me correctly, his name is Rivard. At all events I shall not insist upon passing the item at this time because I realize that it is important to have the information.
As regards the practice mentioned by the hon. member, of permitting contractors to be present when tenders are opened, may I reply that the practice still prevails in the department. All contractors are always welcome. In fact, either the contractors or their representatives are always present when tenders are opened. The practice followed in the time of the hon. member is still pursued.

I am glad to hear that, because there is nothing more necessary than to establish in the public mind a confidence in the reception and disposition of tenders in a department such as the Department of Public Works. I am sure the minister appreciates the importance of what I say.
Mr, CARDIN:	In many instances it is a
protection for the minister.

I am going to ask the
minister to permit the item to stand, and

Supply-Post Office
when it comes up again I should like to have full information on the points upon which I have asked for information, and in relation to this whole innovation. As I said, I should like to have the reasons for it, the effect of it, why it is thought necessary and how it is thought it will improve the practice which has heretofore existed. It seemed to me that all precautions were taken and everything done to satisfy the public in connection with tendering, and I should like to have full information as to why it is thought necessary to have a clerk of tenders.
I quite agree with that.

The minister might also give us such information as he has regarding the appointment of a purchasing agent. The previous government had in mind the establishment of a central purchasing authority, such as we had a long time ago and which sa/ed us hundreds of thousands of dollars. The sale of material was another matter that gave all of us a good deal of difficulty. Perhaps the minister will inform us whether any effort has been made, and if so to what extent, to unify and simplify the matter of purchases by the various departments, because there will be a great deal said as we proceed, especially in connection with one department.

The item might stand.
Item stands.
Departmental administration, including amount required to pay allowances to typists, grade 1, employed cutting stencils, in accordance with regulations approved by order in council, $553,020.
I take it that the minister does not expect to pass this item but just wants to discuss it.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Acting Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I would be quite willing to pass the item if the committee has no objection.
We would hesitate to deprive the minister of an opportunity to talk about his own item.
Could we have some information as to the large increase in the number of employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The committee will notice that there is a decrease in the total item. There is an increase in the staff from 132 in 1937-38 to 150 this year. This is the report:
Additional positions provided in 1938-39 estimates:
Departmental administration-18.
2	stenographers, grade 3 (office of deputy postmaster general).
Additional assistance being required, two positions of stenographer, grade 3 were approved by the civil service commission, and authorized by order in council. The commission then issued promotion certificates on behalf of two permanent employees.
3	stenographers, grade 2 (administrative services) .
2 stenographers, grade 1 (1 in administrative services; 1 in equipment and supply branch).
1 clerk, grade 2 (administrative services).
4	clerks, grade 1 (administrative services).
4	typists, grade 1 (administrative services).
1 packer and helper (equipment and supply branch).
1 office boy (administrative services).
These positions were approved by the civil service commission and authorized by order in council to provide for the permanent appointment through the commission of temporary employees of the same class in the branches named when the restriction on permanent appointments were removed by order in council.
Has there been any reorganization of the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Some temporaries were made permanent.
I mean an internal reorganization of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not think so.
Has there been an increase in the service through air mail or anything of that kind?

I was just going to direct the attention of the Minister of Mines and Resources to page 165 of the estimates where he will find a map draughtsman at $1,800. I told him before that I thought there was another draughtsman somewhere but I could not give it to him at the time. This map draughtsman in the Post Office Department would seem to be a duplication of his heroic effort to minimize duplication.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The explanation I have just received is that that draughtsman does not draw geographical maps.
I am told that there are political maps.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My information is that he draws maps of machinery, but perhaps that may have some connection with politics.

I do not know whether the minister cares to proceed beyond this one item to-night, but there is some information I should like to obtain and I was wondering if I should wait until the Postmaster General returns.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
If my hon. friend would ask the questions, they would be on Hansard.
Supply-Post Office
I would prefer to wait until his return.
I notice there is an amount of $4,080 for a private secretary and then an additional allowance of $600 for the same purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: For many years the arrangement has been that when a private secretary has been in the permanent civil service he retains whatever salary he received and receives an additional allowance of $600 for acting as private secretary. These items do not mean that he receives $600 in addition to the S4.0S0; it means simply that he receives the $600 in addition to his regular salary in the department.
Are these private secretaries still taken care of when the government changes after they have served for three years?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: So far as I remember, the Civil Service Act was amended in 1934 or 1935.
It was amended before the late government came into office.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I was referring to the last amendment. Prior to 1930 a private secretary who had acted as such for a year was privileged to obtain a position in the permanent service of the government at a salary not less than that paid to a principal clerk, or chief clerk, I just forget which. In 1934 the Civil Service Act was amended to provide that before a private secretary could obtain that privilege he would be obliged to serve three years in that capacity. I believe that is the situation at the present time.
Will the minister tell us why this department has to have an " artist, lantern slides?" I was always under the impression that this was all handled by the Department of Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is for publicity purposes. I imagine that a good part of his work would be in connection with the campaign which is put on during the Christmas season, " Post your mail early " and matters of that kind. One frequently sees sketches made by men who are in the habit of putting on lantern slides in the moving pictures.

Who does the necessary
repairs to the various post offices?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is done by the Public Works department.
That being the case, what is the necessity for a mechanical engineer, a senior engineer and an assistant mechanical engineer?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That would be in connection with machines used in post office work.
Will the minister explain the item for supervisor for rest room; where is this rest room, and for whom is it in operation? Is it for employees or visitors?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: There are between four and five hundred women employees in the department at Ottawa, and a rest room has been placed at their disposal just as there are rest rooms in every building in which there are a number of departmental employees. The position of supervisor of rest room was created to look after that.
Has the minister a rest room in his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: So far as the minister is concerned, he works all the time. I do not know what the staffs do, but I shall inquire.
This is another item showing in a certain part a very substantial increase-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: A decrease.

No; an increase. In
administration there is an increase from $278,060 to $298,520, represented by increase in staff. I assume the volume of business going through the Post Office Department has considerably increased during the past year, necessitating that increase in staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
That can be accounted for in two ways. First, there is $11,012 which covers the five per cent deduction. As will be remembered, when other departments have been in supply it has been explained that the comparison with last year's estimates is not quite accurate in that last year, when the main estimates were brought down no provision was made for the five per cent deduction. The estimates came down with the five per cent deduction off all salaries, and later on, during the course of the session, a supplementary estimate was brought down whereby the five per cent was restored. But it was restored in a lump sum and not attributed to the particular departments to which it applied. Therefore, in comparing the $253,000 with the $273,000 one must take account of the salary deduction of $11,000 odd. In other words, there is a difference of approximately $9,000, which is accounted for by the eighteen extra employees whom I mentioned a moment ago; and the fact that the revenue of the post office has increased by $1,300,000, as compared with last year, would account for the increase.

Supply-Post Office

I ought to voice a protest
against this method of bringing down the post office estimates. Two years ago, when the estimates of this department were brought before us, there was a lengthy discussion in the committee regarding the manner in which the department submitted its estimates. I am not disputing the accuracy of the estimates, but the idea was that anyone examining the estimates as they have been submitted and are now being submitted cannot tell what they mean. One does not know what the estimates in themselves indicate; no one can get from them anything definite except that the expenditures estimated for the coming year are so many millions of dollars. Possibly there is a little more business than there was last year, but in the discussion we had in this chamber in the session of 1936 the Postmaster General gave an undertaking to the committee that in submitting future estimates he would bring down a statement of the sort which is submitted by any business executive to the shareholders of a company. In these estimates as we have them we can get no idea of what the business of the post office was for the past year or what it is likely to be for the coming year. We cannot tell from the estimates whether the department has made a profit or has been running at a loss. All we are asked to do is to vote the estimates in the absence of any substantial information. I should like to know why the the undertaking given by the Postmaster General two years ago has not been carried out, namely, that in subsequent years we should have a proper statement from which we might get a better understanding of the operations of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The hon. member will find
a great improvement in the manner in which the estimates arS presented this year as compared with last year. Last year there were two items for the whole business of the post office; this year there will be found at least seven or eight. This year, under the item which we are now considering, departmental administration, there are given complete details of the persons employed in departmental administration. Last year that was all bulked, and it was impossible for members of the committee to ascertain exactly what w'as being done. I am familiar with the hon. gentleman's criticism. He would like the Post Office Department to give a profit and loss statement as any business would do. After all, this is one of the largest departments of public business, and he would like to have a statement of profit and loss showing rentals, cost of carrying mails, newspapers and so on. Do 1 understand that to be what the hon. gentleman has in mind?
More or less.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I can give that to some
extent. A condensed comparative summary of the revenue of the Post Office Department and expenditure for the year ended March 31, 1937, and that estimated for the year 1938 will show: Revenue, postage stamps, cards, etc., sold for 1936-37: 828,179.322.60; estimated for 1937-38: S28.720.000. Postage paid in cash, 1936-37: S10.203,389.06; estimated for 1937-38: $10,882,000. All other revenue, 1936-37, S2.798,854.69; estimated 1937-38, $2,97S,500. The gross revenue for 1936-37 is S41,181,566.35, and the estimated revenue for 1937-38 is 842,580.500. Deductions from revenue, 1936-37, postmasters' commissions and allowances, 86,384,055.93; discount to stamp vendors, special deliveries, transit charges and so forth, $522,958.42; making a total for 1936-37 of 86,907,014.35. 1937-38 estimates: Deductions from revenue, postmasters' commissions and allowances, S6,738,700; discounts to stamp vendors, special deliveries, transit charges, etc., 8561,300; making an estimated total for 1937-38 of 87,300,000. Expenditures : 1936-37: Salaries, 816,187,668.62; mail service 813.526,697.60; miscellaneous, 8830,209.05; total of 830,538,575.27; 1937-38: Salaries, 87,448,938; mail service, $13,944,415; miscellaneous, 8850,000; total, $32,243,378. 193637: Excess of revenue over outside services, $3,735,973; for 1937-38, 83,037,122.
Is that the net post office estimated profit for the ensuing year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No. Next are the Public Works department charges. Although this is only a bookkeeping entry it is about $2,700,000. Rental value of post office space, including char service, fuel and light, amounts to S2,750,000.
WThat is the net result?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I wish to give just a few other items if my right hon. friend will permit me. We make an estimate of some credit items which should be given to us: Credit for franking privilege, 81,122,676; credit for the operation of the savings bank, SSO.OOO. So that the surplus as given is $3,037,122.
Does that include repairs to buildings?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Repairs to buildings are all done by the Public Works department. I should imagine that the public works charge is all-inclusive, because I see here it includes
Supply-Post Office

char service, fuel and light; it also includes charges for repairs, furniture and all that kind of thing which goes into the work of the post office.

That does not answer the question I asked at first. Although the minister has given us the figures as the department has them, I do not see any good reason why a properly prepared statement in the form of an actual balance sheet of the utility as such, could not be submitted to the committee. I do not believe any hon. member, by cursorily listening to the figures just submitted by the acting Postmaster General, can make out what these figures really mean. He tells us there is a profit of something over a million dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: A surplus of 83,037,122.
Is that after deducting the amount which the Department of Public Works charges for the use of buildings?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No.

Well, then, the profit is not quite as large as is suggested by the acting Postmaster General. He has given us the credit side of the balance sheet; but he has forgotten to put down some of the debit items, one of which I shall mention at once. The Post Office Department obtains each year an enormous revenue from stamps which really should not be credited to that department.
On cheques.

On cheques, yes. All stamps used for excise purposes which go to the revenue of the post office should be credited to the revenue of some other department. It is almost impossible to ascertain the value of the stamps which are used each year in Canada for excise purposes. If that were put against the credit items enumerated by the minister this evening, it would be extremely difficult to say whether the post office is operating at a profit or at a loss. Even with the opportunity of examining the figures as submitted by the post office we are unable to say whether it is making a profit. I am anxious that the post office, which is perhaps the largest utility operating in the dominion, should be carried on in the same manner as any well conducted enterprise would be; and it seems to me that the minister, instead of submitting the series of figures which have been presented this evening, should present a proper balance sheet each year showing the exact amount of the revenues, from what sources they have been derived, the expenditures, what they are for, and a comparison

with previous years. I had expected that, as this matter was discussed in this chamber at considerable length a couple of years ago and the Postmaster General gave an undertaking that such a course would be followed, within a period of two years the post office would be able to adjust itself to that new form of bookkeeping which we were led to believe they would give to the committee, and I do not understand why after this lapse of time it is not forthcoming. Could the minister inform us what stands in the way of the presentation of a proper statement in the form of a balance sheet, whereby at a moment's glance hon. members would know how the post office had been operating during the past twelve months and what would be the estimated expenditures and revenues for the ensuing year? Can the minister give us any assurance that next year something of the sort can be submitted to us, we having waited already for two years?

If the hon. member will turn to the auditor general's report, Post Office Department, part P 2, and read the thirty pages between pages 2 and 32, he will find the information he seeks. But what I cannot understand is why we could not in these estimates detail the revenues and expenditures with as much particularity as they are in the auditor general's report. The report of the auditor general gives a complete statement of the revenues of the Post Office Department for the year ended March 31, 1937. In volume I there is a broad statement of it; but in volume II, which I hold in my hand, are the details. According to the auditor general, the Post Office Department for the year ended March 31, 1937, had a gross revenue of 841,181,566.35. To earn that gross revenue it was necessary to make expenditures out of the revenue as received, and those expenditures which are also stated at page 2 covered rent allowances, commissions, discounts, postage on parcels to other countries, indemnities, etc., showing a total of 86,907,014.35. The difference between that sum and the gross revenue to which I have just referred amounts to 834,274,552, being the total of net postal revenue for the year. Then follow the particulars of the expenditures made. And at page 32 of the auditor general's report there is the complete detail- that is complete under large headings-of what is on the thirty pages before that, showing that the total expenditures of the department were S31.906.272.05. Now the difference between that sum and 834.274,552, it will be observed, is something like 82,300.000. That

Supply-Post Office
is the auditor general's report. Why the Post Office Department should show a different statement here this evening I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speechtext: Yes; that is the correct figure according to the auditor general's report, but that is not the figure the minister gave this evening. I assume that was through error, because he was dealing with the sum he has just mentioned together with another sum which should not have been included.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I might recapitulate: Excess of revenue, S3.735,976.73-and here perhaps is where the difference comes in-headquarters administration and contingencies, $1,341,756, leaving a net surplus of $2,394,220.73. I am informed that the dominion government does not take into consideration the overhead, which would be represented by headquarters administration and contingencies. That would perhaps be the explanation, although I do not think it will satisfy my right hon. friend.

The auditor general's report we know to be accurate, because it is vouched for by the production of documents. What the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) said, and what I desire to support him in, is that we were to have before us not a statement such as we have now but a statement in connection with the post office estimates which would show the contemplated revenue from all sources, and the contemplated expenses broken up in much the same form as they are broken up here. In the estimates presented to us they are broken up, but not broken up under headings such as you find on page 32 of the auditor general's report. For instance, civil government, at Ottawa and outside; then travelling expenses amounting to $70,000; general expenses, materials, supplies, repairs, etc., $357,000; printing and stationery, $454,000. Then there is other outlay, that is payments to the rail companies for handling mail and to the air lines and steamship companies, and finally you have the total under the words "total expenditure," amounting to $31,906,272.05.
What the hon. member for Winnipeg North is seeking is that there should be in these estimates, as I believe it was understood there would be for the year 1938, a record indicating the contemplated revenues, not in detail of course but under the broad headings used in the auditor general's report. It is necessary to have that 'before one can arrive at any idea as to what the net revenue will be, because from the gross revenue derived from sale of stamps, etc., one has to deduct the amount which has to be spent immediately
for the purpose of earning that money, namely, transport and matters of that kind. That leaves a balance. Then there was some additional casual revenue represented by $3,470.76 and fines and forfeitures, $171. The broad general statement will be found in volume I of the auditor general's report, Post Office Department. I say that because it has always been thus under all governments. Do not for a moment think that I am charging this administration with having done anything that was not done by previous governments. I am not suggesting that for a moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have not suggested that as an alibi, either.
No, but that would come presently-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No, I thought of it a long time ago.

-in fact immediately if I resumed my seat. But I desire to point out that all that is sought is something which is not new in this house. When the present acting minister was sitting on this side I can recall the unpleasant hours that the then Postmaster General spent waiting anxiously for a Friday night on which the call went out, "Night or Blucher." Very often it used to be both "night" and "Blucher." Under those circumstances it is nothing new when I say that successive governments have been grappling with that question. The hon. member for Winnipeg North put it up to the minister whether we could not make a statement something similar to this, perhaps not with so much detail, indicating our contemplated or expected revenues, the expenditures that we are appropriating, because the auditor general is bound to take the credits item by item and show what has happened to the money thus voted by parliament. The minister is quite right when he says that great objection was taken to that large item amounting to many millions in which everything was included, in other words, a basket item. That item was objectionable to this house, and that was the grievance urged by the hon. member for Winnipeg North upon the government I think two years ago, this government with a new mandate from the people to lower the tariff and increase the taxes. In that glorious day they were to give us all the information we sought and indicate so large a surplus that we might increase the salaries of the rural mail carriers and provide satisfactory jobs for all those who desire to displace Conservatives. My hon. friend the surveyor (Mr. Fafard) laughs, because I can see that he knows perfectly
Supply-Post Office

well, having mapped out the rural mail routes in his district, how great the difficulty is to provide for all these things in the manner that we anticipate before we get into office.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The manner to which our people are accustomed.

To which your people are accustomed; that may be. I suggest that it would not be difficult to show the relation of the contemplated expenditure to this contemplated revenue in the manner indicated. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North says, this is a utility. It stands on an entirely different basis from any other department.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
On that point, without at all
wishing to draw a red herring across the trail, but by way of digression, may I make this statement, that in my own department I found that against certain items we could place a revenue item. For instance, for the vetcraft shops I am obliged to ask parliament for something like $72,000, whereas really there is income of something like $50,000 to set off against it. The net loss would be about $25,000. Something similar occurs with reference to the sick mariners' fund, as my right hon. friend knows. I tried to make some arrangement with the treasury board to show in the estimates that there is a revenue coming in. I suppose the principle would apply to some extent in connection with the matter we are now discussing. It would be an estimated income. But I was informed that though this is done in Great Britain-
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: -that against the appropriation there is an estimated revenue, this has never been the practice in Canada; and for some reason, which frankly I have not been able to understand, we are not permitted to enter in our estimates proposed or estimated revenue.
The reason is that the money is paid direct to the consolidated revenue fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: And it does not come into the department; but if my right hon. friend would permit me to say so, I know of a case where it is not done.
So do I.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Where it would not be done.
We might exchange confidences.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It is not a confidence. In the case of vetcraft, at the end of the year, or at a certain period of the year, when large sums of moneys are expended on poppies

and the returns from the poppy sales have not come in, the department runs very short of money, and in order to pay the salaries of the men employed in the vetcraft shops it would be necessary to obtain a governor general's warrant unless substantial sums were voted in the estimates prior to that time. But the money returns to the department. When the cheques come in from sales of poppies the money returns to the department. Perhaps that is a confidence, but I do not think so.

I am not going to take up too much time on this matter, but I might point out to the minister that the auditor general's report shows the total of the postal revenue for the year and indicates the heads under which that revenue is received. Then he gives the total gross revenue and the disbursements that are made from revenue, in other words the money that is spent from day to day for the purpose of earning that revenue, and this is given under half a dozen heads. That, it seems to me, would be possible in our estimates without difficulty; it is just what the minister has in his estimates now, plus half a page, for instance, merely indicating the estimated revenue during the year, just as has been done by the auditor general in his report. In the one instance we have the exact revenue and in the other we would have merely the contemplated revenue.
There might be one difficulty about that, and it might be a very considerable difficulty. If it should be contemplated that the postal rate should be reduced from three to two cents, and it should appear in the estimates in that form, it would anticipate the budget and therefore might lead to some difficulty. The minister has succeeded in breaking the estimate up partly in comparison with what it has been in the past, but it seems to me there would not be much difficulty in breaking it up into those items into which the auditor general has divided it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is broken up to some extent, as my right hon. friend knows, in the main estimates, and in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North I have given further details. I could go still further and give him an estimate of the revenue for the year 1938 under each heading, such as postage stamps, second-class matter, third-class matter, metered mail and 60 on.

That is just what the hon. member says we were to have printed, rather than depend upon the statement of the minister.

Supply-Post Office

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My right hon. friend has been of this much assistance to me-and possibly he has put his finger on the real reason why this is not stated in the estimates-that at some time or another it may be proposed by the Minister of Finance either to reduce or to increase the rate on mail, and it would be impossible for the Postmaster General to make any estimate without divulging that fact.
He gave up $800,000 on United States magazines without consulting us.

I am generally in accord with this desire to have a proper business accounting in the Post Office Department, but I heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North refer to rents as one of the expenditures made in carrying on the business of the post office. I should like to hear whether the hon. gentleman desires the rents on all post offices to be assessed and recorded, because, if so, I cannot see how that can be done on a purely utilitarian basis, which is the only basis on which it could possibly enter into the post office account.
As a matter of fact, it does not enter into it at all in the auditor general's report.
I am raising the question.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North on several occasions has brought forward this same query. Evidently he desires, as I know other hon. members also desire, to know how far the Post Office Department pays its way, whether there is a surplus or a deficit.
There are two or three factors which must be taken into consideration in addition to those mentioned by the minister. For instance, a post office building is required. It is constructed by the Department of Public Works, out of moneys voted for that purpose. It is maintained by the Public Works department, no charge being made to the Post Office Department and no details of expenditure appearing in the accounts of that department. Then the building is heated, and the cost of heating is paid out of a vote under the Public Works department for the maintenance of public buildings. There is also furniture, which to a considerable extent is supplied in the same way, from a vote for furnishings and supplies for public buildings. So if the hon. member for Winnipeg North were to get all this information, which I think it would be impossible to obtain, I fancy he would find that the Post Office Department does not carry itself, does not pay its way. I do not think there is any doubt about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am inclined to agree with my hon. friend. In those circumstances the Post Office Department could not carry itself. Then very probably there would be some contra accounts. Very often in a post office building there are offices occupied by the customs department or half a dozen other departments. I know in my own city the Department of National Defence has offices in the post office; the department of health, the Department of Public Works and the Department of Justice also have offices in that building. There are half a dozen departments with offices in the post office in Quebec city, and I should imagine that the same condition obtains in a great many other localities. So I think the accounting would be difficult; I think -the hon. member for Winnipeg North would admit that.

Yes; but I was under the impression that two years ago, when this matter was raised in the house, the Postmaster General undertook to obtain a proper accounting from the Public Works department, to find out what would be the rental value of all these buildings.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I should imagine that the figures I gave in response to the request of my hon. friend are those which the Postmaster General of the day agreed to obtain.

I think the minister is quite correct: I believe those figures which have been submitted to us to-night, amounting to about 82,750,000, were probably obtained as a result of negotiations between the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works. I have always had a strenuous objection to the way in which our post office buildings have been built. The Department of Public Works builds post offices, and then says to the Post Office Department, "Here are some buildings for you whether you wan'-them or whether you do not."

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Oh, no.

Oh, yes. I make that definite statement, knowing the facte in one particular case, where a post office was erected for the Post Office Department, which post office that department did not want. I believe that is not the only case of that kind, because in the past post offices have been erected without any request on the pant of the postal authorities, and I believe we had the promise last year or the year -before that that state of affairs would be rectified. I hope it has been, and I hope that in the future no post office will be ereoted in any part of the Dominion of Canada unless it is at the request of the postal authorities themselves. It is quite

Supply-Post Office

possible that if the Post Office Department were to have the say in the erection of these post offices this item of $2,750,000 might be considerably less. I do not know whether there has been any experience during the past twelve months, but perhaps the minister might say whether during thait time the Post Office Department have been asked to take over buildings, for which no requests have come in from that department itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I am informed that there
have not been, so far as we know. In any case, I shall be very glad to transmit the hon. member's observations to the Post Office Department. Meanwhile I would ask that the item stand.

I should like to ask a question with respect to practice in the department. Last summer postal station L on St. Clair avenue, at the comer of Appleton and St. Clair, was moved from that location to a point about 500 feet east, on the opposite side of the street, from one ward to another. Through what means was that move made?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am informed that this discussion might more properly come under another item, namely the item respecting salaries and other expenses, staff and so on.

What number was the
last one?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We are now on item No. 257. I would suggest that the discussion of the matter would come under item No. 25S.

That is satisfactory.
Item stands.
Lands, parks and forests branch-branch administration, $23,460.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this branch of the Department of Mines and Resources comes under the head of lands, parks and forests branch, and I believe I might briefly outline to the committee the functions of this particular branch. In the first place, it has to do with the government of the northwest territories.
Is this the only item respecting the northwest territories?

The item called is not. I am just giving a brief survey of the work of the branch. It has to do with the government of the northwest territories, and that is again subdivided into the eastern arctic and western arctic divisions. It

has also to do with the government of the Yukon territory. Likewise, the branch is engaged in what is known as the dominion forest service. It is true that the forest lands are all owned by the provinces; but as hon. members will recall, the federal government has several forest experimental stations, and the administration of these come under this branch.
Then, there are forest products laboratories, one of which is in British Columbia, another in Ottawa and another, more definitely related to the pulp and paper industry, in the city of Montreal. Then, there is the matter of land registry. All the ordnance lands, admiralty lands and public lands, indeed, all the lands of the federal government which are not directly administered by other departments, such as the Department of National Defence, are administered by the Department of Mines and Resources, and come under the direction of this branch.
Under this item?

No; I am just giving a general survey. We shall come back to particulars in a minute. In addition, there is the administration of national parks in Canada. I believe at the present time there are about twenty of them. Likewise, there is the administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act. This briefly summarizes the work of the particular branch whose estimate we are about to consider.
Item No. 135 has to do with branch administration, including such matters as the salary of the director, and his immediate assistants. Indeed, it might be described as a sort oi head office item for this branch of the department.

Item agreed to.
Government of the northwest territories- general administration, operation, maintenance and improvement of services, including Wood buffalo park, $245,320.
Would the minister give an account of the reindeer experiment?

The reindeer experiment appears to be working out satisfactorily. The herd is now more than 4,000 in number, and each fall a certain number are being slaughtered. The meat is distributed to some of the schools and hospitals at Aklavik, and also to the natives. I understand the skins are also utilized by the natives for clothing. From the information we have received so far, I believe that as the years go by the experiment will prove a very useful contribution to the natives of that region.

Supply-Mines and Resources
Some consideration is being given to getting the Eskimos interested in small reindeer herds of their own, so that they may be used, as in Lapland, as beasts of burden. The economy of Lapland I am told is largely dependent upon the reindeer, and I think it is possible that this might be repeated among our Eskimos in the north. To the extent that we succeed, we are making them more selfreliant and able to fend for themselves. At the present time the experiments look promising. A few Eskimo boys are being trained as herdsmen, and are being taught how to look after these animals.
Are the reindeers being protected? Is the Eskimo permitted to hunt them?
No; at the present time the reindeer are herded, and they are under supervision.
The journey has been completed, has it not?
Yes.
How many are there now?
I stated a moment ago there were something over 4,000.
Could the minister give us a report on the buffalo that were returned to the range around Fort Vermilion? I believe they were taken from the buffalo park at Wainwright some years ago.

They appear to be doing quite well. Those buffalo are partly in the northwest territories and partially in the extreme northern part of Alberta. It is very difficult to get an accurate census of the buffalo, but as nearly as the park wardens can estimate there are upwards of 8,000.

Are they drifting south
at all?

I suppose they overrun the boundaries of the park at times, but the park is very large and contains suitable pasturage. It is really the natural habitat of these animals. There are some wood buffalo there and as a matter of fact they do not tend to migrate to the south. I suppose if the herd were to increase to 100,000 or so, they would overrun the greater part of Alberta.
I notice there is an increase from $32,000 to $49,000 in supplies and materials; could the minister explain this increase?

There would be medical supplies, additional food and fuel and equip-51952-464
ment for the medical officers and provisions for the destitute. I notice that that particular item is $10,000.
That would make up the increase?

Not altogether. There are years when the fur catch is quite light and the authorities say that at the present time we are in a low fur cycle. Under these circumstances the Indians, the Eskimos and the half-breeds have to be assisted and the requirements are greater. Only a week or so ago I had a telegram from a party who had just returned from Aklavik who painted a rather dark picture of conditions there. I do not think they are quite as bad as reported, but there is no doubt that the shortage of fur has a bearing upon the amount of supplies and relief necessary to be sent into the north country.
That explanation would also cover the increase in the amount for hospitalization?
It would have a bearing upon that. When the natives are poorly nourished they are more susceptible to disease and there are more calls on our hospital accommodation.
I notice the hotels and shops in different parts of Canada have been selling buffalo meat, and I should like to know if there is any revenue from this sale.

There would be none in connection with the Wood Buffalo park in northern Alberta. Over 2.000 buffalo were slaughtered this year at Wainwright and Elk island. I think there were something like
5.000	or 6.000 in the Wainwright park alone. The park was overstocked, and it was a question of either extending the area and spending a good deal of money on fences, or reducing the herd by slaughter. It was considered that about 4,000 buffalo were sufficient for the purposes for which the park was created, and the surplus animals were slaughtered and the meat sold. The hides from this slaughter have been sold. The revenue derived from these sales will go into the consolidated revenue fund. While I am on this point I might direct the attention of hon. members to page 10 of the report of the Department of Mines and Resources where will be found a statement of the revenue turned into the consolidated revenue fund by the department for the fiscal year ended March 31 last.

It is set out in the auditor general's report.
Supply-Mines and Resources
Have any buffalo been sold to parks in the United States or in other parts of the world?
A couple of years ago a small shipment of half a dozen was sent to Germany, but there are no sales made.

Has the question of
whether the Eskimo is an Eskimo or an Indian been decided yet?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That
question is before the supreme court.
I have been urging my colleague, the Minister of Justice, to secure a decision on that matter as quickly as possible as we are a little at controversy with the province of Quebec.

Has the case been
argued?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
Is the buffalo meat sold by tender or by other negotiations?
By advertised tender.
What is the population of the northwest territories?
Approximately 1,500 white people, 4,000 Indians and 5,000 Eskimos.
How is that population divided between the two districts?
The greater number is in the Mackenzie river country. There are very few Indians in the eastern arctic, the population being principally Eskimos.
Who was the successful tenderer this year for the buffalo meat? This meat was on sale in nearly all the towns in Saskatchewan.

Burns and Company. I
am informed, were the highest tenderers and got the meat and the hides also.
How many tenders were received for the buffalo meat?

I believe there were two,
but I cannot recall at the moment the other tenderer. Both, however, were from packing companies.
Are the Eskimos of Canada self-supporting, or are they quite a burden on the Canadian government?

We have given them
relief steadily during the last few years.

In the western arctic,
broadly speaking west of Hudson bay, in the

Mackenzie river country, they are pretty well self-supporting; they do not require a great deal of assistance from the government. Unfortunately, that is not the case to the same degree in the eastern arctic, and it is the eastern arctic that constitutes the main burden of relief so far as the Eskimos are concerned.

There is an item of
854,810 for hospitalization, professional and other services, grants to schools, assistance to industrial homes; and for the year 193738 the amount was 851,460. Could the minister give the detailed expenditures under this item last year?

There has been some increase in pupils in the schools, and that involves additional grants for educational work. There was an increase in the number of pupils in the school at Aklavik and there have been a few additional nurses who have been sent in for hospital work.

I did not make myself
quite clear. What I wanted was not so much an explanation of the way in which the money was to be expended as a detailed statement of the actual expenditures made- the amounts to various institutions and organizations, and so on.
The total amount estimated for this year for hospitals is S19,500, which is an increase of S2,500 over the previous year.
What I am more interested in is a statement giving the details of the expenditure in the past year-to what organizations the money was paid and how it was expended.

I do not think I have that information in detail. There are hospitals. for instance, in the western arctic, at Fort Smith. Hay river and Fort Simpson. There are two at Aklavik, and in the eastern arctic, one at Chesterfield and one at Pangnirtung. The expenditures for these I gave a moment ago. The figure is S19.500, which is an increase as compared with last year. Then, there is maintenance of patients in provincial sanatoria and maintenance of those in provincial asylums. Individuals who become insane or become mental cases have to be sent out of the territory to institutions where they can be cared for. In this case they go to a provincial institution and their maintenance has to be taken care of. There is transportation of patients and there are other transportation charges, besides freight, cartage and express. At a score of points

Supply-Mines and Resources
(here are schools which have to be maintained. The supplies for these schools and transportation of these supplies make up the item.

Can the minister give
any further details of the expenditure for the past year showing those to whom the amounts were paid?
I have not that information under my hand, but a note will be taken of the question and the information can be supplied.
What proportion of the population of the northwest territories is white, and is there any demand on the part of that population for representation in this chamber?
There are 1,500 whites, it is estimated.
That is in the whole of the northwest territories?
Yes; and so far I have not heard of any suggestion that they should be represented in parliament.
A bill was introduced into this house. These people are virtually disfranchised, and while the population is not large in comparison with the Yukon, it is not very small.

It is smaller than in the Yukon. At any rate, so far as I am aware, during my period of office here no request of the kind has come. Since this question has been raised, it may be interesting to observe there is a probability of there being a substantial increase in the white population in the western arctic during the next few years. One of the most promising fields potentially for gold mining has been discovered north of Great Slave lake, eight hundred miles north of Edmonton. I visited that area last September. One mine is going into operation shortly, and another is in process of construction. From present indications it would appear that there is a possibility of a considerable mining development in that country. That, of course, will increase the population and create problems in administration. I may say for the information of the committee that this is now receiving the consideration of the officers in the department. We desire if possible to see ahead the problems that may arise and prepare as far as we can for them. While so far there has not been, to my knowledge, any request from that area for representation in this parliament, I should not be surprised if it did arrive within a few years.
How will supplies go in to that new field?
North of Slave lake? Down the Athabaska river. It will go by railway from Edmonton to Waterways, which is the terminus of what I think is called the Northern Alberta railway.
It is the old Alberta and Great Waterways.

The old Alberta and Great Waterways, now operated by the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. From Waterways by boat down to Fitzgerald; from Fitzgerald by portage for sixteen miles to Fort Smith; that is over the rapids on the Slave river.
No; but the minister is now describing the way in. I thought he spoke of a new field to the north, again, of this one.
No; I am coming to that. From Fitzgerald to Smith on the Slave river; down the Slave river to Slave lake, and across Slave lake to these mining areas on the northern side.
Does the minister mean the Peace river instead of the Slave river?

No; I am speaking about the Athabaska and Slave rivers. It may be of interest to the committee to have this information about the development which has taken place in that country. I should suppose that five years ago the total amount of freight moved from Waterways down the Athabaska river probably did not exceed 350 or 400 tons. Last year 22.000 tons of freight moved down this river.
I did not think it was under this item that transportation facilities to the north country would be discussed.

No. M3r hon. friend is
quite right. It will come up under another item. I am merely giving the information in response to a question.

I see that "sundries" have risen considerably, from $2,733 to $4,030. "Sundries" seem to be a place where considerable increases can be put in without exposing anything. Can the minister give details of how this larger amount has been made up?

That is an unallotted vote; it is a sort of general blanket vote put in for contingencies. I stated a moment ago that a considerable development had tak'"- place

Supply-Mines and Resources
in this territory. It is not possible to foresee every item of expense that may be required, and consequently we thought it wise to increase this sundries vote rather more than a thousand dollars so that we would have something to fall back upon in case there arose the need for expenditures that at the present moment cannot be foreseen. It is difficult to tell what may arise in a district which is eight hundred miles north of Edmonton, to say nothing of the distance it is from the capital of the dominion.

That is quite all right, but the item considered as a percentage seems to be a large amount. Here we have an increase from $2,733 to $4,030, or nearly fifty per cent added to the amount expended last year under sundries. I think this item deserves more attention, and I should like to have a little more information about it.
I suggest to the committee that an increase of $1,300 is not an unreasonable amount. Of course, $1,300 is $1,300.
That is right. When one is talking in millions it does not mean much. I quite understand that.

But when one is talking of the development of a vast area of country it does not, I think, mean very much. I repeat that it is quite impossible to foresee every item or kind of expense that may arise in the next year; and we thought it wise-and I trust the committee will approve our judgment-to increase the item by the amount that my hon. friend has mentioned. After all, $1,300 is not very much when one considers the responsibilities that may arise there.

I ask again,
Can we be given any idea of the principal items of which this vote will be made up? That is all. It is $1,300.
My hon. friend is referring to the sundries item?
Yes.

No; I cannot at the moment. We may have an epidemic of smallpox, or measles, or something of the kind which will have to be looked after. It might be that a number of people will go crazy in that country and will have to be brought out to a mental institution. Any one of half a dozen things of that general sort might happen.
It is too bad that the minister did not think of that last year when he brought down his estimates.
We may have erred last year.

In the last few months there have been various statements by the premier of British Columbia to the effect that he was going to extend that province to include the Mackenzie river basin. Would the minister tell the committee whether there have been any negotiations with this end in view or negotiations of any kind dealing with the matter of that province taking over the Mackenzie river basin?
That is, the extension of the boundaries to the arctic?
Yes.

No. I understand the
premier of British Columbia recently gave out a statement at some future date he was going to make that request to the federal government, but so far as I am aware he has made no official request to the government.
There has been no request made to date?
In respect to the extension of the boundaries of eastern British Columbia to the arctic?
Yes.
There was, of course, in respect to the Yukon.
But there has been no request made in regard to the Mackenzie river district?

No. It might have been
mentioned in a letter to the Prime Minister -I am not sure about that-but it has not been to me. I know that Mr. Pattullo made a statement the other day in Vancouver or somewhere else in British Columbia to the effect that he intended to request that the boundaries of the province should be extended to the arctic.
There are no negotiations under way at the present time?

No.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
